Expectimax Tree​

  • White Node: Choose action with max value.
  • Black Node: Average state values of all possible actions.
  • Compute Optimal Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) values for the current state by construction an expectimax tree.
Q(s,a)=∑s′Pν(s′∣s,a)[Rν(s,a,s′)+γV(s′)]Q(s,a)=\sum_{s'}P_\nu(s'|s,a) \left[R_\nu(s,a,s')+\gamma V(s')\right]Q(s,a)=s′∑​Pν​(s′∣s,a)[Rν​(s,a,s′)+γV(s′)] V(s)=max⁡aQ(s,a)V(s)=\max_a Q(s,a)V(s)=amax​Q(s,a)
  • Pν(s′∣s,a)P_\nu(s'|s,a)Pν​(s′∣s,a): Transition probability.
  • Rν(s,a,s′)R_\nu(s,a,s')Rν​(s,a,s′): Expected Reward
  • V(s′)V(s')V(s′): Value of the next state.

Limitations of Expectimax Tree​

O((∣S∣×∣A∣)H)O((|\mathcal S|\times|\mathcal A|)^H)O((∣S∣×∣A∣)H)
  • Scaling Exponentially with Depth: Tree size grows exponentially with depth HHH.
  • ∣S∣|\mathcal S|∣S∣: Number of possible states.
  • ∣A∣|\mathcal A|∣A∣: Number of possible actions.
  • HHH: Depth of the tree.

Monte Carlo Search Tree, MCTS​

  • Given a model μv\mu_vμv​
  • Build a search tree rooted at the current state sts_tst​, sample actions and next states.
  • Iteratively Construct and update the tree by performing KKK simulation episodes starting from the root node.
  • Once search is finished, select the current action with maximum value in the search tree.

at=arg⁡max⁡a∈AQ(st,a)a_t = \arg\max_{a \in A} Q(s_t, a)at​=argmaxa∈A​Q(st​,a)

AspectMCTSExpectimax Tree
ExpansionConstruct partial search treeConstruct full search tree up to a given depth
ExplorationSelect branches using UCBExplore all possible branches
EvaluationEstimate values using sampled returnsCalculate expected values using transition probabilities
Action SelectionSelect actions based on estimated valuesSelect actions with maximum expected values
Computational CostControlled by simulation budgetExponential in search depth
Trade-offMore efficient, but approximateMore exhaustive, but computationally expensive

Tree Traversal​

Q(s,a,i)=Vi⏟Exploitation+cln⁡n(s)n(s,a)⏟ExplorationQ(s,a,i) = \underbrace{V_i}_{\text{Exploitation}} + \underbrace{c\sqrt{\frac{\ln n(s)}{n(s,a)}}}_{\text{Exploration}}Q(s,a,i)=ExploitationVi​​​+Explorationcn(s,a)lnn(s)​​​​
  • Use Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) to select which branches to explore.
  • ccc: Exploration coefficient.
  • n(s)n(s)n(s): Number of visits to state sss.
  • n(s,a)n(s,a)n(s,a): Number of visits to state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a).
  • Exploration Bonus: Encourages selecting less-visited actions.
  • UCB: Balances exploitation of high-value actions and exploration of less-visited actions.
    • In bandit problems, ccc is a constant to balance exploration and exploitation.

Node expansion​

  • Add a new child node to the search tree for an unexplored action.

Rollout​

  • Perform a random simulation from the expanded node until termination or a depth limit.
  • Calculate the total return from the simulation.
ROLLOUT(Si)Loop: if Si is a terminal return Sielse Ai=random available action SiSi=Simulate (Ai,Si)\begin{aligned} & \text{ROLLOUT}(S_i) \\ & \quad \text{Loop: } \\ & \quad \quad \text{if } S_i \text{ is a terminal } \\ & \quad \quad \quad \text{return } S_i \\ & \quad \quad \quad \text{else } \\ & \quad \quad \quad \quad A_i = \text{random available action } S_i \\ & \quad \quad \quad \quad S_i = \text{Simulate } (A_i, S_i) \\ \end{aligned}​ROLLOUT(Si​)Loop: if Si​ is a terminal return Si​else Ai​=random available action Si​Si​=Simulate (Ai​,Si​)​

Backpropagation​

  • Propagate the simulation return back through the selected path to the root.
  • Update visit counts and estimated values of the visited nodes.

Advantages of MCTS​

  • Highly Selective Best-First Search
  • Evaluates states dynamically, unlike DP.
  • Use Samples to break curse of dimensionality.
  • Works for "black box" model.
  • Computationally efficient.

Reinforce Learning with Human Feedback, RLHF​

Why Human Feedback?​

  • Some tasks do not have clear or automatically measurable rewards.
  • Humans can provide:
    • Preferences: Choose between two outputs (A > B).
    • Rankings: Rank multiple outputs (1st, 2nd, 3rd).
    • Evaluations: Judge whether an answer is better or worse.
  • Example: Evaluating which chatbot response is more polite.

Alignment Problem​

  • LLMs are pretrained to predict text, not necessarily to generate useful responses.
  • Generated text may be harmful, biased, or factually incorrect.
  • Traditional evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU) do not directly capture human preferences.
  • Human feedback helps align model behavior with human preferences for helpfulness, truthfulness, and safety.
  • Example: A model may generate plausible but impractical coding advice.

Core Idea of RLHF​

  • Human Feedback: Use human evaluations and preferences to guide model training.
  • Alignment: Align model behavior with human expectations and preferences.
  • Optimization: Train models to maximize rewards reflecting human preferences rather than only next-token likelihood.
    • Goal of LLM's pretraining: max⁡θ∑tlog⁡Pθ(xt∣x<t)\max_\theta \sum_{t}\log P_\theta(x_t | x_{<t})maxθ​∑t​logPθ​(xt​∣x<t​)
      • Maximize the likelihood of the next token.
    • Goal of RLHF: max⁡θEy∼πθ(⋅∣x)R(x,y)\max_\theta \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot|x)} R(x, y)maxθ​Ey∼πθ​(⋅∣x)​R(x,y)
      • Maximize the expected reward of human-preferred responses.
  • Application: Widely used in NLP and LLM alignment.

RLHF Training Pipeline​

Pre-training → SFT → Reward Model Training → RL Optimization

  1. Pre-training: Train a base model on a large text corpus using next-token prediction.
  2. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Fine-tune the base model on high-quality instruction-response examples.
  3. Reward Model Training: Train a reward model using human-labelled preferences to predict response quality.
  4. Reinforcement Learning: Optimize the model's policy to maximize rewards predicted by the reward model.

Step 1. Pre-training​

  • Select a base model pretrained on a massive text corpus.
  • Learns general knowledge and language patterns.
  • Limitation: May produce biased, unsafe, or irrelevant responses.

Step 2. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)​

  • Goal: Train the base model to follow instructions and generate reasonable responses.
  • Collect high-quality demonstration data (instruction, input, output).
  • Fine-tune the base model on the curated dataset.
  • Limitation: Instruction-following does not guarantee alignment with human preferences.

Step 3. Reward Model Training​

  • Goal: Learn a reward function that reflects human preferences.
  • Generate multiple responses for the same prompt.
  • Humans compare or rank the responses.
  • Train a reward model to assign scores based on human preferences.
  • Example: A professional, polite response (B) is preferred over a blunt response (A): B > A.
  • Outcome: Convert human judgments into numerical reward scores.

Step 4. RL with Human Feedback​

  • Goal: Optimize the LLM policy using the trained reward model.
  • Algorithm: PPO (example).
  • Generate responses using the current policy.
  • Score responses using the reward model from Step 3.
  • Update the policy to maximize reward.
  • Use a KL penalty to limit deviation from the reference policy and reduce over-optimization.
    • KL Penalty: Penalizes large deviations between the updated policy and the reference policy.
    • Higher KL Penalty → More conservative policy updates.
DKL(P∥Q)=∑xP(x)log⁡P(x)Q(x)D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}DKL​(P∥Q)=x∑​P(x)logQ(x)P(x)​ max⁡θ[E[R(x,y)]−βDKL(πθ∥πref)]\max_\theta\left[ \mathbb E[R(x,y)] -\beta D_{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) \right]θmax​[E[R(x,y)]−βDKL​(πθ​∥πref​)]
StrategyCNNLLM
Feature ExtractionFreeze backbone, train classifier headFreeze base model, train task-specific head
Partial Fine-TuningFreeze early layers, update selected layersPEFT (e.g., LoRA): Freeze base weights, train small additional parameters
Full Fine-TuningUpdate all pretrained weightsUpdate all pretrained weights (not PEFT)

Chatgpt​

Benefits of RLHF​

  • Alignment: Aligns model behavior with human values and preferences.
  • Safety & Usefulness: Encourages safer, more useful responses with higher human acceptance.
  • Ambiguous Goals: Handles tasks where rewards are difficult to define explicitly.

Challenges of RLHF​

  • Cost: Requires extensive human annotations, making training expensive.
  • Human Bias: Biases in human feedback can be transferred to the reward model and policy.
  • Over-optimization: Models may exploit the reward function rather than produce genuinely better responses (Reward Hacking).
  • Scalability: Collecting and applying human feedback becomes difficult as models and tasks scale.

Applications of RLHF​

  • ChatGPT: Improvement in safety and helpfulness
  • Claude: Constitutional AI for more nuanced alignment
  • Gemini: Large-scale RLHF for multimodal capabilities
  • Robotics: Learning task from human demonstrations
  • Teaching robots via human feedback to cook
  • Medical AI systems trained with doctor's feedback to align with human expert medical standards.

Policy Search Methods​

Instead of VVV and QQQ functions, we directly estimate the optimal policy.

πθ(a∣s)≈P(a∣s,θ)\pi^{\theta}(a|s) \approx P(a|s, \theta)πθ(a∣s)≈P(a∣s,θ)

  • Policy was generated directly from the value function (e.g. ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy)
  • Parameterize the policy directly.
    • Instead of v(s,w)v(s,w)v(s,w) or q^(s,a,w)\hat{q}(s,a,w)q^​(s,a,w), we have πθ(a∣s)\pi^{\theta}(a|s)πθ(a∣s)
    • Given a particular state sss, what actions should we take? (What is probability of that particular action?)
    • θ\thetaθ is a learnable parameter which could be a neural network.

Value-based and Policy-based Methods​

  • Value-based: Learnt value function, Implicit policy (e.g. ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy)
  • Policy-based: No value function, Learnt policy.
    • Good convergence properties
    • Effective in high-dimensional or continuous action spaces
      • if it is really continuous and large, it is not efficient as well.
    • Can learn stochastic policies.
    • Sometimes policies are relatively simple, values and models are complex.
    • Typically reaches local optima.
    • Obtained knowledge is specific and does not generalize well.
  • Actor-Critic: Learnt value function, Learnt policy.

Policy Gradient Techniques​

  • Trust-Region Based: Optimize the policy in a trust zone (closer circle).

Stochastic policies​

Rock-Paper-Scissors​

  • A deterministic policy is easily exploited
    • Deterministic policy: If we follow a set of action or sequence of actions, we will definitely reach the goal and will always reach teh same location.
  • A uniform random policy is optimal policy.

Grid World​

ϕ(s,a)=(1010⏟walls,0100⏟actions)\phi(s,a) = \big(\underbrace{1 0 1 0}_{walls}, \underbrace{0 1 0 0}_{actions}\big)ϕ(s,a)=(walls1010​​,actions0100​​)
  • Agent cannot differentiate between the grey states.
  • ϕ(s,a)\phi(s,a)ϕ(s,a) features describing state sss and action aaa.
  • ϕ(s,E)=(1,0,1,0⏟NESW,0,1,0,0⏟NESW)\phi(s,E) = (\underbrace{1, 0, 1, 0}_{\text{NESW}}, \underbrace{0, 1, 0, 0}_{\text{NESW}})ϕ(s,E)=(NESW1,0,1,0​​,NESW0,1,0,0​​) is the North and the South are walls and the agent will move to the East.
  • If π(grey)=W\pi(\text{grey}) = Wπ(grey)=W, then when the agent is in the left grey state, it will move west, get stuck in a loop, and never reach the goal.

  • Therefore, an optimal stochastic policy moves randomly EEE or WWW in grey states.
    • πθ(wall to N and S, move E)=0.5\pi_{\theta}(\text{wall to N and S, move E}) = 0.5πθ​(wall to N and S, move E)=0.5
    • πθ(wall to N and S, move W)=0.5\pi_{\theta}(\text{wall to N and S, move W}) = 0.5πθ​(wall to N and S, move W)=0.5
  • The agent will reach the goal with high probability.
  • Policy-based methods can learn Stochastic policies. 4563

Given a policy πθ(a∣s)\pi_{\theta}(a|s)πθ​(a∣s) with parameters θ\thetaθ, the goal is to find the best θ\thetaθ.

J1(θ)=vπθ(S1)J_1(\theta) = v_{\pi_{\theta}}(S_1)J1​(θ)=vπθ​​(S1​)
  • In an episodic task (with an end state), J1(θ)J_1(\theta)J1​(θ) is for that particular start state and measures how much expected return we can get.
  • S1S_1S1​ is the start state.
  • J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ) is the measure of the quality of the policy or the objective function to optimize.

  • In continuing environments (doesn't have an end state), consider the states and take the average value weighted by how often the agent visits each state.

Policy-based Methods​

  • Policy-based RL is an optimization problem, find θ\thetaθ that maximize J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ).
    • J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ) is the policy objective function.
  • Gradient-free methods: Hill Climbing, Genetic Algorithms, ...
  • Gradient-based

Δθ=α∇θJ(θ)\Delta{\theta} = \alpha \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta)Δθ=α∇θ​J(θ)

  • Policy gradient method will search for a local minimum in J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ) by ascending the gradient of the Policy.
    • why ascending? because we want to maximize the objective function's value/rewards.
    • ∇θJ(θ)=(∂J(θ)θ1⋮∂J(θ)θn)\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\theta_1} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\theta_n} \end{pmatrix}∇θ​J(θ)=​θ1​∂J(θ)​⋮θn​∂J(θ)​​​
    • α\alphaα is the step size.
ΔθJ(θ)=∇θEd[vπθ(s)]\Delta{\theta} J(\theta) = \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_d[v_{\pi\theta}(s)]ΔθJ(θ)=∇θ​Ed​[vπθ​(s)]
  • Assume the policy πθ\pi_{\theta}πθ​ is differentiable.
  • Compute an estimate of the policy gradient.
  • Compute ΔθJ(θ)\Delta{\theta} J(\theta)ΔθJ(θ) using Monte Carlo samples since we need to explore the environment, gather information, and then learn the policy.

  • Assume the policy πθ\pi_{\theta}πθ​ is differentiable.

Policy Gradient Theorem​

Policy Gradient = How policy changes ×\times× How good the action is.

  • It generalizes the likelihood ratio approach to multi-step MDPs.
  • Replaces the instantaneous reward r(s,a)r(s,a)r(s,a) with the action value function Qπθ(s,a)Q^{\pi\theta}(s,a)Qπθ(s,a).
    • s1→a1s2→a2s3→a3Goals_1 \xrightarrow{a_1} s_2 \xrightarrow{a_2} s_3 \xrightarrow{a_3} \text{Goal}s1​a1​​s2​a2​​s3​a3​​Goal
 ∇θJ(θ)=Eπθ[∇θlog⁡πθ(s,a)⏟Score FunctionQπθ(s,a)⏟Action Value Function]\ \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi\theta}[ \underbrace{\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s,a)}_{\text{Score Function}} \underbrace{Q^{\pi\theta}(s,a)}_{\text{Action Value Function}} ] ∇θ​J(θ)=Eπθ​[Score Function∇θ​logπθ​(s,a)​​Action Value FunctionQπθ(s,a)​​]
  • The theorem applies to start state objective, average reward, and average value objectives.
  • Qπθ(s,a)Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)Qπθ​(s,a): the expected long-term reward starting from state sss, taking action aaa and following policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​
  • ∇θlog⁡πθ(s,a)\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s,a)∇θ​logπθ​(s,a): How sensitive the policy is to changes in θ\thetaθ.
  • Eπθ[⋅]\mathbb{E}{\pi\theta}[\cdot]Eπθ[⋅]: Average over all possible states and actions according to the policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​.
  • ∇θJ(θ)\nabla_\theta J(\theta)∇θ​J(θ): The direction in which θ\thetaθ should be changed to increase the objective J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ).

Simplified Policy Gradient steps​

  1. Loop
  2. Collect trajectories for Policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​
  3. Estimate advantage function AAA
  4. Compute Policy Gradient g^\hat{g}g^​
  5. Update Policy Parameter θnew=θold+αg^\theta_{\text{new}} = \theta_{\text{old}} + \alpha \hat{g}θnew​=θold​+αg^​
  • g^\hat{g}g^​ is the estimated policy gradient.
    • Can be MC policy gradient, or Actor-Critic Policy Gradient.
  • if α\alphaα is too big, data collected under bad policy and it cannot be recovered.
  • if α\alphaα is too small, it is not efficient use of experience.

REINFORCE Algorithm​

  • Monte Carlo Policy Gradient: explore and learn from the environment and learn the optimal policy.
  • Update Parameters by Stochastic Gradient Ascent.
  • Using policy gradient theorem: find the partial derivatives to find the direction of the gradient.
  • Using return vtv_tvt​ as an unbiased sample of Qπθ(s,a)Q^{\pi\theta}(s,a)Qπθ(s,a).
    • Qπθ(st,at)=Eπθ[vt∣st,at]Q^{\pi\theta}(s_t,a_t) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi\theta}[v_t | s_t, a_t]Qπθ(st​,at​)=Eπθ​[vt​∣st​,at​]

Δθ=α∇θlog⁡πθ(st,at)vt\Delta{\theta} = \alpha \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s_t,a_t) v_tΔθ=α∇θ​logπθ​(st​,at​)vt​

Function REINFORCEInitialize θ arbitrarilyfor each episode {s1,a1,r1,…,sT−1,aT−1,rT}∼πθ dofor t=1 to T−1 doθ←θ+α∇θlog⁡πθ(st,at)vtreturn θ\begin{array}{l} \textbf{Function REINFORCE} \\ \qquad \text{Initialize } \theta \text{ arbitrarily} \\ \qquad \textbf{for each episode } \{s_1,a_1,r_1,\ldots,s_{T-1},a_{T-1},r_T\} \sim \pi_\theta \textbf{ do} \\ \qquad\qquad \textbf{for } t=1 \textbf{ to } T-1 \textbf{ do} \\ \qquad\qquad\qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s_t,a_t) v_t \\ \qquad \textbf{return } \theta \\ \end{array}Function REINFORCEInitialize θ arbitrarilyfor each episode {s1​,a1​,r1​,…,sT−1​,aT−1​,rT​}∼πθ​ dofor t=1 to T−1 doθ←θ+α∇θ​logπθ​(st​,at​)vt​return θ​

REINFORCE: Sutton and Barto​

Input: a differentiable policy parameterization π(a∣s,θ)Algorithm parameter: step size α>0Initialize policy parameter θ∈Rd′ (e.g., to 0)Loop forever (for each episode):Generate an episode S0,A0,R1,…,ST−1,AT−1,RT, following π(⋅∣⋅,θ)Loop for each step of the episode t=0,1,…,T−1:G←∑k=t+1Tγk−t−1Rk(Gt)θ←θ+αγtG∇ln⁡π(At∣St,θ)\begin{array}{l} \textbf{Input: } \text{a differentiable policy parameterization } \pi(a \mid s,\theta) \\ \textbf{Algorithm parameter: } \text{step size } \alpha > 0 \\ \textbf{Initialize } \text{policy parameter } \theta \in \mathbb{R}^{d'} \text{ (e.g., to 0)} \\ \\ \textbf{Loop forever (for each episode):} \\ \qquad \text{Generate an episode } S_0,A_0,R_1,\ldots,S_{T-1},A_{T-1},R_T, \text{ following } \pi(\cdot \mid \cdot,\theta) \\ \qquad \textbf{Loop for each step of the episode } t=0,1,\ldots,T-1: \\ \qquad\qquad G \leftarrow \sum_{k=t+1}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-1}R_k \qquad (G_t) \\ \qquad\qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \gamma^t G \nabla \ln \pi(A_t \mid S_t,\theta) \end{array}Input: a differentiable policy parameterization π(a∣s,θ)Algorithm parameter: step size α>0Initialize policy parameter θ∈Rd′ (e.g., to 0)Loop forever (for each episode):Generate an episode S0​,A0​,R1​,…,ST−1​,AT−1​,RT​, following π(⋅∣⋅,θ)Loop for each step of the episode t=0,1,…,T−1:G←∑k=t+1T​γk−t−1Rk​(Gt​)θ←θ+αγtG∇lnπ(At​∣St​,θ)​
  • Slow to converge.
  • Going to have low bias but high variance.

Actor-Critic​

  • Actor has a supervisor (Critic) that tells it how good or bad the action actor took is.
  • Actor: Controls agent's behavior using Policy-based methods.
  • Critic: Measures how good the action taken by the agent is using Value-based methods.

Reducing Variance using a Critic​

Qw(s,a)≈Qπθ(s,a)Q_w(s,a) \approx Q^{\pi\theta}(s,a)Qw​(s,a)≈Qπθ(s,a)

  • Monte Carlo policy gradient has high variance.
  • Use a Critic to estimate the action-value function.
  • Actor-Critic algorithms maintains two sets of parameters:
  • Critic: Updates action-value function parameters www.
    • It is solving the problem of policy evaluation.
    • How good is the policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ for current parameters θ\thetaθ?
    • MC or TD methods to estimate the value function.
  • Actor: Updates policy parameters θ\thetaθ in the direction advised by the Critic.
ΔθJ(θ)=Eπθ[∇θlog⁡πθ(s,a)Qw(s,a)]Δθ=α∇θlog⁡πθ(s,a)Qw(s,a)\Delta_{\theta} J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi\theta}[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s,a) Q_w(s,a) ] \\ \Delta_{\theta} = \alpha \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s,a) Q_w(s,a)Δθ​J(θ)=Eπθ​[∇θ​logπθ​(s,a)Qw​(s,a)]Δθ​=α∇θ​logπθ​(s,a)Qw​(s,a)
  • It follows an approximate policy gradient.

Action-Value Actor-Critic​

  • Using Linear value function approximation: Qw(s,a)=ϕ(s,a)TwQ_w(s,a) = \phi(s,a)^T wQw​(s,a)=ϕ(s,a)Tw
  • Critic: Use Linear TD(0) to update www.
  • Actor: Use policy gradient to update θ\thetaθ.

  • δ\deltaδ is Critic.
  • θ\thetaθ is Actor.
  • Update www: Critic can provide a better advice.

TRPO, Trust Region Policy Optimization​

A(s,a)=Q(s,a)−V(s)A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s)A(s,a)=Q(s,a)−V(s)

  • Advantage: the difference between the Q and the V values.
    • How good is an action compared to the average action for a specific state.
  • Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) = the expected long-term return when taking action aaa in state sss
  • V(s)V(s)V(s) = the expected average long-term return when following the policy from state sss
  • Used in many Deep RL algorithms such as TRPO, PPO, GRP and etc.
  • Stationary Target: Fixed target during training.

Update the old policy to a new policy such that they are with in a "Trusted" distance apart.

  • Conservative policy update allows improvement instead of degradation of policy.
  • Improve training stability by avoiding parameter updates that changes the policy too much at one step.
  • By enforcing KL divergence constraint on size of the policy update at each iteration.

Kullback-Leibler Divergence​

KL divergence score

KL(P∣∣Q) KL(P || Q)KL(P∣∣Q)

  • It quantifies how much one probability distribution differs from another probability distribution.
  • ∣∣||∣∣ indicates divergence or PPP's divergence from QQQ.

DKL(P∣∣Q)=∑x∈XP(x)log⁡P(x)Q(x)D_{KL}(P || Q) = \sum_{x \in X} P(x) \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}DKL​(P∣∣Q)=∑x∈X​P(x)logQ(x)P(x)​

  • Given two probability distributions PPP and QQQ over a discrete random variable XXX, the KL divergence is the expected value under PPP of the log ratio between PPP and QQQ.
    • Multiplying by P(x)P(x)P(x) gives more weight to events that occur frequently under PPP.
    • PPP large, QQQ small → large divergence
    • PPP small, QQQ large → effect is smaller
  • e.g. πold(a1∣s)=0.8\pi_{\text{old}}(a_1|s) = 0.8πold​(a1​∣s)=0.8 and πold(a2∣s)=0.2\pi_{\text{old}}(a_2|s) = 0.2πold​(a2​∣s)=0.2, while πnew(a1∣s)=0.1\pi_{\text{new}}(a_1|s) = 0.1πnew​(a1​∣s)=0.1 and πnew(a2∣s)=0.9\pi_{\text{new}}(a_2|s) = 0.9πnew​(a2​∣s)=0.9
    • The policy changed drastically in one update step.
  • TRPO prevents this by enforcing DKL(πold∥πnew)≤δD_{KL}(\pi_{\text{old}} \| \pi_{\text{new}}) \leq \deltaDKL​(πold​∥πnew​)≤δ.

TRPO vs Gradient Descent​

ComparisonGradient DescentTrust Region
Optimization approachPicks the steepest direction.Defines a region in which to search for the next point.
StepMoves forward by a step size.Determines the maximum step size to explore.
Next pointMoves directly in the selected direction.Locates the optimal point within the trust region.
Search processRepeats the directional step.Resumes the search from the selected point.
Main characteristicFast and simple for optimizing an objective function.Controls how far the optimization explores at each step.
In Reinforcement LearningMay not work well in reinforcement learning.Provides a restricted region for finding the next optimal point.

PPO, Proximal Policy Optimization​

  • TRPO is relatively complicated, every time we need to find trust region and solve the optimization problem, leading to high computational cost.
  • PPO simplifies it by using a Clipped Surrogate function
  • Based on a ratio of two policies
    • Current Policy πθ\pi_{\theta}πθ​
    • Baseline Policy (Old Policy) πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}πθold​​

Policy Ratio​

rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st)r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t|s_t)}rt​(θ)=πθold​​(at​∣st​)πθ​(at​∣st​)​
  • rt(θ)=1r_t(\theta)=1rt​(θ)=1: no policy change
  • rt(θ)>1r_t(\theta)>1rt​(θ)>1: the action becomes more likely
  • rt(θ)<1r_t(\theta)<1rt​(θ)<1: the action becomes less likely

The surrogate objective is:

J(θ)=Et[rt(θ)A^t]J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ r_t(\theta)\hat A_t \right]J(θ)=Et​[rt​(θ)A^t​]
  • A^t>0\hat A_t>0A^t​>0: the action was better than expected → increase its probability.
  • A^t<0\hat A_t<0A^t​<0: the action was worse than expected → decrease its probability.
  • Without a restriction, the policy may change too much in a single update.

Clipped Surrogate Objective​

JCLIP(θ)=E^t[min⁡(rt(θ)A^t⏟Normal Policy Gradient objective,clip⁡(rt(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)⏟Clipped Policy Gradient ObjectiveA^t)]J^{CLIP}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb E}_t \left[ \min ( \underbrace{r_t(\theta)\hat A_t}_{\text{Normal Policy Gradient objective}}, \underbrace{\operatorname{clip} (r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}_{\text{Clipped Policy Gradient Objective}}\hat A_t ) \right]JCLIP(θ)=E^t​​min(Normal Policy Gradient objectivert​(θ)A^t​​​,Clipped Policy Gradient Objectiveclip(rt​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​​A^t​)​
  • rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st)r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t|s_t)}rt​(θ)=πθold​​(at​∣st​)πθ​(at​∣st​)​ is the ratio of the new policy to the old policy.
  • A^t=Q(st,at)−V(st)\hat A_t = Q(s_t,a_t) - V(s_t)A^t​=Q(st​,at​)−V(st​) is the advantage function.
  • ϵ\epsilonϵ is a hyperparameter, usually 0.10.10.1 or 0.20.20.2.
  • If ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2ϵ=0.2, the clipping range is [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2].
  • For A^t>0\hat A_t>0A^t​>0, PPO removes the benefit of increasing rtr_trt​ above 1+ϵ1+\epsilon1+ϵ.
  • For A^t<0\hat A_t<0A^t​<0, PPO removes the benefit of decreasing rtr_trt​ below 1−ϵ1-\epsilon1−ϵ.
  • The policy ratio itself is not strictly forced to remain inside the clipping range.
  • Instead, clipping removes the incentive for excessively large beneficial policy updates.

Algorithm: PPO with Clipped ObjectiveInput: θ0, ϵfor k=0,1,2,… doCollect set of partial trajectories Dk on policy πk=π(θk)Estimate advantages A^tπk using any advantage estimation algorithmCompute policy updateθk+1=arg⁡max⁡θLθkCLIP(θ)by taking K steps of minibatch SGD (via Adam), whereLθkCLIP(θ)=Eτ∼πk[∑t=0Tmin⁡(rt(θ)A^tπk,clip⁡(rt(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^tπk)]\begin{array}{l} \textbf{Algorithm: PPO with Clipped Objective} \\ \textbf{Input: } \theta_0,\ \epsilon \\ \textbf{for } k=0,1,2,\ldots \textbf{ do} \\ \qquad \text{Collect set of partial trajectories } \mathcal{D}_k \text{ on policy } \pi_k=\pi(\theta_k) \\ \qquad \text{Estimate advantages } \hat{A}_t^{\pi_k} \text{ using any advantage estimation algorithm} \\ \\ \qquad \text{Compute policy update} \\ \qquad \theta_{k+1} = \arg\max_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\theta_k}^{CLIP}(\theta) \\ \\ \qquad \text{by taking } K \text{ steps of minibatch SGD (via Adam), where} \\ \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\theta_k}^{CLIP}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_k} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{T} \min \left( r_t(\theta)\hat{A}_t^{\pi_k}, \operatorname{clip} \left( r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon \right) \hat{A}_t^{\pi_k} \right) \right] \\ \end{array}Algorithm: PPO with Clipped ObjectiveInput: θ0​, ϵfor k=0,1,2,… doCollect set of partial trajectories Dk​ on policy πk​=π(θk​)Estimate advantages A^tπk​​ using any advantage estimation algorithmCompute policy updateθk+1​=argmaxθ​Lθk​CLIP​(θ)by taking K steps of minibatch SGD (via Adam), whereLθk​CLIP​(θ)=Eτ∼πk​​[∑t=0T​min(rt​(θ)A^tπk​​,clip(rt​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^tπk​​)]​

Function Approximation​

v^(s,w)≈vπ(s)\hat{v}(s, \mathbf{w}) \approx v_\pi(s)v^(s,w)≈vπ​(s)

  • Incremental methods for prediction
  • Model-free VFA: MC and TD targets

GPI, Generalized Policy Iteration​

  • Iterate between policy evaluation and policy improvement
  • Policy Evaluation: Approximate policy evaluation. q^(⋅,⋅,w)≈qπ\hat{q}(\cdot, \cdot, \mathbf{w}) \approx q_\piq^​(⋅,⋅,w)≈qπ​
  • Policy Improvement: ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy policy improvement.

Types of Action-Value FA​

s→FA(w)→q^(s,w)s \to \text{FA}(\mathbf{w}) \to \hat{q}(s, \mathbf{w})s→FA(w)→q^​(s,w)
  • State Value Function Approximation
(s,a)→FA(w)→q^(s,a,w)(s, a) \to \text{FA}(\mathbf{w}) \to \hat{q}(s, a, \mathbf{w})(s,a)→FA(w)→q^​(s,a,w)
  • Action Value Function Approximation

    • q^(s,Right,w)=8.7\hat{q}(s, \text{Right}, \mathbf{w}) = 8.7q^​(s,Right,w)=8.7

  • The network output is a vector of Q-values for each action.
  • More convenient to use discrete action spaces.

Action VFA​

q^(s,a,w)≈qπ(s,a)\hat{q}(s, a, \mathbf{w}) \approx q_\pi(s, a)q^​(s,a,w)≈qπ​(s,a)

  • Approximate the Action-value function.
  • Doing action aaa at state sss, Approximate the Q-value of that action.

J=Eπ[(qπ(s,a)−q^(s,a,w))2]\mathcal{J} = \mathbb{E}_{\pi} \left[ (q_\pi(s, a) - \hat{q}(s, a, \mathbf{w}))^2 \right]J=Eπ​[(qπ​(s,a)−q^​(s,a,w))2]

  • Minimize mean-squared error (MSE) between the approximate Q-value q^(s,a,w)\hat{q}(s, a, \mathbf{w})q^​(s,a,w) and the true Q-value qπ(s,a)q_\pi(s, a)qπ​(s,a).

Δw=α(qπ(s,a)−q^(s,a,w))∇wq^(s,a,w) \Delta \mathbf{w} = \alpha (q_{\pi}(s,a) - \hat{q}(s,a,\mathbf{w})) \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \hat{q}(s,a,\mathbf{w})Δw=α(qπ​(s,a)−q^​(s,a,w))∇w​q^​(s,a,w)

  • Use SGD to find the local minimum.
  • qπ−q^q_{\pi} - \hat{q}qπ​−q^​ tells us how much the prediction is off from the target.
  • ∇wq^(s,a,w)\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \hat{q}(s,a,\mathbf{w})∇w​q^​(s,a,w) tells us how each weight affects the predicted QQQ-value.

Linear Action VFA​

x(s,a)=[x1(s,a)x2(s,a)⋮xn(s,a)]x(s, a) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1(s, a) \\ x_2(s, a) \\ \vdots \\ x_n(s, a) \end{bmatrix}x(s,a)=​x1​(s,a)x2​(s,a)⋮xn​(s,a)​​
  • Feature vector is used to represent the state and action pair.

q^(s,a,w)≈x(s,a)Tw=∑jxj(s,a)wj\hat{q}(s, a, w) \approx x(s, a)^T w = \sum_j x_j (s, a) w_jq^​(s,a,w)≈x(s,a)Tw=∑j​xj​(s,a)wj​

  • Predicted Q-value is a linear combination of the feature values. (sum of each feature value xjx_jxj​ multiplied by the weight wjw_jwj​)
q^(s,a,w)=x(s,a)Twq^=x1w1+x2w2+⋯+xnwn\begin{aligned} \hat{q}(s, a, w) = x(s, a)^T w \\ \hat{q} = x_1w_1 + x_2w_2 + \cdots + x_n w_n \end{aligned}q^​(s,a,w)=x(s,a)Twq^​=x1​w1​+x2​w2​+⋯+xn​wn​​
  • x1,x2,⋯x_1, x_2, \cdotsx1​,x2​,⋯: features of the state and action pair.
  • w1,w2,⋯w_1, w_2, \cdotsw1​,w2​,⋯: weights that need to be learned.
  • derivative q^\hat{q}q^​ with respect to www.
    • ∂q^∂w1=x1\frac{\partial \hat{q}}{\partial w_1} = x_1∂w1​∂q^​​=x1​
    • ∂q^∂w2=x2\frac{\partial \hat{q}}{\partial w_2} = x_2∂w2​∂q^​​=x2​
∇wq^=[x1x2⋮xn]=x(s,a)\nabla_w\hat{q} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix} = x(s, a)∇w​q^​=​x1​x2​⋮xn​​​=x(s,a)
  • e.g. q^=2w1+5w2\hat{q} = 2w_1 + 5w_2q^​=2w1​+5w2​, then ∇wq^=[25]\nabla_w\hat{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}∇w​q^​=[25​]
Δw=α(qπ−q^)∇wq^=α(qπ−q^)x(s,a)=α(qπ(s,a)−q^(s,a,w))x(s,a)\begin{aligned} \Delta w \\ &= \alpha (q_{\pi} - \hat{q}) \nabla_w\hat{q} \\ &= \alpha (q_{\pi} - \hat{q}) x(s, a) \\ &= \alpha (q_{\pi}(s, a) - \hat{q}(s, a, w)) x(s, a) \end{aligned}Δw​=α(qπ​−q^​)∇w​q^​=α(qπ​−q^​)x(s,a)=α(qπ​(s,a)−q^​(s,a,w))x(s,a)​

Incremental Prediction Algorithm​

  • Assumption so far: qπ(s,a)q_{\pi}(s,a)qπ​(s,a) is given.
  • But an actual RL agent does not know the true qπ(s,a)q_{\pi}(s,a)qπ​(s,a).
  • Therefore, we need to estimate a target.
  • Monte Carlo (MC): the target is the return GtG_tGt​.
    • Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+⋯G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \cdotsGt​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+⋯
    • Update: Δw=α(Gt−q^(st,at,w))∇wq^(st,at,w)\Delta w = \alpha \bigl(G_t - \hat q(s_t,a_t,w)\bigr)\nabla_w\hat q(s_t,a_t,w)Δw=α(Gt​−q^​(st​,at​,w))∇w​q^​(st​,at​,w)
    • It compares the predicted Q-value with the actual return observed after the episode.
    • MC does not use another prediction inside the target.
  • Temporal Difference (TD): the target is Rt+1+γq^(st+1,at+1,w)R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1},w)Rt+1​+γq^​(st+1​,at+1​,w).
    • Update: Δw=α(Rt+1+γq^(st+1,at+1,w)−q^(st,at,w))∇wq^(st,at,w)\Delta w = \alpha \bigl(R_{t+1} + \gamma\hat q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1},w) - \hat q(s_t,a_t,w)\bigr)\nabla_w\hat q(s_t,a_t,w)Δw=α(Rt+1​+γq^​(st+1​,at+1​,w)−q^​(st​,at​,w))∇w​q^​(st​,at​,w)
    • It compares the current Q prediction with the current reward plus the discounted next Q prediction.
    • Bootstrapping: update the current prediction using another prediction.
    • Because the next prediction can also be wrong, we ask: can repeated updates converge to a stable value?
  • On-policy: behavior policy = target policy.
  • Off-policy: behavior policy ≠\ne= target policy.
    • The policy that generates the experience is different from the policy that we want to evaluate or improve.

Batch Methods​

  • Incremental learning: an experience -> update the weights.
  • Batch methods: collect experiences -> store in D\mathcal{D}D -> reuse D\mathcal{D}D for training.
  • It seeks to find the best fitting value functions.

D={(s1,v1π),(s2,v2π),⋯ ,(sN,vNπ)} \mathcal{D} = \{(s_1, v^{\pi}_1), (s_2, v^{\pi}_2), \cdots, (s_N, v^{\pi}_N)\}D={(s1​,v1π​),(s2​,v2π​),⋯,(sN​,vNπ​)}

  • Which www makes v^(s,w)\hat{v}(s, w)v^(s,w) fit all stored data best?
    • Using the agents' experience or training data.
    • Training data: a fixed batch of previously collected data.

Least Squares Prediction​

  • Given a value function approximation: v^(s,w)≈vπ(s)\hat{v}(s,w) \approx v^\pi(s)v^(s,w)≈vπ(s)
  • Given experience data: D={(s1,v1π),(s2,v2π),…,(sN,vNπ)}\mathcal{D} = \{(s_1,v_1^\pi),(s_2,v_2^\pi),\ldots,(s_N,v_N^\pi)\}D={(s1​,v1π​),(s2​,v2π​),…,(sN​,vNπ​)} consisting of state-value pairs.
LS(w)=∑t=1N(vtπ−v^(st,w))2LS(w)=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(v_t^\pi-\hat{v}(s_t,w)\right)^2LS(w)=t=1∑N​(vtπ​−v^(st​,w))2
  • LS(w)LS(w)LS(w) is the sum of all squared prediction errors.
  • The Least Squares method finds the parameter vector www that minimizes the squared error between v^(s,w)\hat v(s,w)v^(s,w) and vπ(s)v^\pi(s)vπ(s).
wπ=arg⁡min⁡wLS(w)w^\pi=\arg\min_w LS(w)wπ=argwmin​LS(w)
  • If we use the mean squared error instead:
ED[(vtπ−v^(st,w))2]=1N∑t=1N(vtπ−v^(st,w))2\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal D} \left[ \left(v_t^\pi-\hat v(s_t,w)\right)^2 \right] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \left(v_t^\pi-\hat v(s_t,w)\right)^2ED​[(vtπ​−v^(st​,w))2]=N1​t=1∑N​(vtπ​−v^(st​,w))2
  • The factor 1/N1/N1/N does not change the minimizing www.

SGD Procedure​

  1. Sample a {state,value}\{\text{state},\text{value}\}{state,value} pair from D\mathcal DD.
  2. Apply the SGD update:
Δw=α(vπ−v^(s,w))∇wv^(s,w)\Delta w = \alpha \left(v^\pi-\hat v(s,w)\right) \nabla_w\hat v(s,w)Δw=α(vπ−v^(s,w))∇w​v^(s,w)
  • Sample from D\mathcal DD -> calculate the error -> update www -> repeat.
  1. Under appropriate conditions, SGD converges toward the Least Squares solution.
  • Then, what model should represent v^(s,w)\hat v(s,w)v^(s,w)?
    • Linear function approximator
    • ANN
    • CNN

DNN, Deep neural network​

  • Universal function approximator
    • Linear FA limited to linear combinations of features v^(s,w)=x(s)Tw\hat{v}(s, w) = x(s)^T wv^(s,w)=x(s)Tw
    • DNN can represent non-linear mappings of features. s→DNN(w)→v^(s,w)s \rightarrow \text{DNN}(\mathbf{w}) \rightarrow \hat{v}(s, \mathbf{w})s→DNN(w)→v^(s,w)
  • Combination of both Linear and Non-Linear transformations
    • z=Wx+bz = Wx + bz=Wx+b
    • h=ReLU(z)h = \text{ReLU}(z)h=ReLU(z)
  • It may require exponentially less nodes or parameters to represent the sample Linear function.
  • SGD can be used to learn parameters
    • prediction -> loss -> gradient -> SGD -> www update.
  • It can generalize from observed states to unseen states.
  • It can handle continuous state spaces, which are common in real world problems.
    • s=(x,y,velocity,angle)s = (x, y, \text{velocity}, \text{angle})s=(x,y,velocity,angle)
    • s=(2.371,5.826,0.43,⋯ )→DNN→v^(s,w)s = (2.371, 5.826, 0.43, \cdots) \rightarrow \text{DNN} \rightarrow \hat{v}(s, \mathbf{w})s=(2.371,5.826,0.43,⋯)→DNN→v^(s,w)
  • E2E learning (learn feature representation and policy together) can be more effective.
  • Function approximation using images, environments with visual observations.
  • DNNs can directly process pixel data and learn from raw images.
  • DNNs can be used in environments with continuous action spaces for approximating policies (Robotics)
  • It can achieve SOTA performance in several complex tasks.

CNN, Convolutional neural network​

  • CONV is the first layer to extract features from an input image.
    • Core building block of a CNN
    • A number of filters such as Edge Detectors are applied to the input image.
  • Padding: add extra pixels around the image to handle edge cases.
    • Valid Padding: no padding, output size is smaller than input size.
      • p=0p = 0p=0.
      • Output size: (n−f+1)×(n−f+1)(n - f + 1) \times (n - f + 1)(n−f+1)×(n−f+1)
      • fff: filter size.
    • Same Padding: add padding so that output size is the same as input size.
      • p=f−12p = \frac{f-1}{2}p=2f−1​
  • Stride: the number of pixels the filter moves across the input image.
    • S=1S = 1S=1: Move the filter by one pixel horizontally and vertically.
    • S=2S = 2S=2: Move the filter by two pixels horizontally and vertically.
  • POOL: down sampling operation which reduces the dimensionality of a matrix.
    • It reduces the number of parameters for large image but retain the valuable information.
    • Max pooling: Max(7, 8, 9, 10) = 10
    • Average pooling: Avg(7, 8, 9, 10) = 8.5
    • Sum pooling: Sum(7, 8, 9, 10) = 34
  • FC: The output matrix after convolution layer is flattened and feed into a fully connected layer similar to ANN.
    • It's a traditional Multi-layer Perceptron/Neural Network.
    • For multi-class classification, Softmax activation function is usually used.
    • Output of the CONV and POOL layers represent a high-level features of the Input image.
    • FC layer uses this feature to classify the input image into the desired class.

Deep Reinforcement Learning​

  • Use DNNs to represent
    • Value and Q-Value function (Action-value function)
    • Policy (Policy Gradient methods)
    • Model
  • Use SGD to optimize loss function.
  • RL makes the target, SGD trains DNN to fit the target.
  • In TD: Δw=learning rate×TD error×gradient\Delta w = \text{learning rate} \times \text{TD error} \times \text{gradient}Δw=learning rate×TD error×gradient
    • TD error: Rt+1+γq^(st+1,at+1,w)⏟Target−q^(st,at,w)⏟Current Prediction\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{q}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1},w)}_{\text{Target}} - \underbrace{\hat{q}(s_t,a_t,w)}_{\text{Current Prediction}}TargetRt+1​+γq^​(st+1​,at+1​,w)​​−Current Predictionq^​(st​,at​,w)​​
  • In Q-Learning: max⁡a′Q(st+1,a′,w)\max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a',w)maxa′​Q(st+1​,a′,w) is the target.

Q-Learning with VFA​

  • Original Q-Learning converges to the optimal Q∗(s,a)Q^*(s, a)Q∗(s,a) using look-up table.
  • VFA Q-Learning minimizes MSD Loss by SGD using target Q estimates instead of true Q.
    • so it can diverge due to the correlation between samples or Non-stationary targets.

DQN​

DQN in Atari​

  • E2E learning of Q(s,a)valuesfrompixelsQ(s,a) values from pixels Q(s,a)valuesfrompixelss$
  • Input state sss is a stack or raw pixels from last 4 frames.
  • Output is Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) for 18 joystick/button positions
  • Reward is chance in score for that step.
  • Network Architecture and hyper-parameters are fixed across all games.
  • 4x84x84 stack of 4 previous frames -> 16 8x8 filters CONV -> 32 4x4 filters CONV -> 256 hidden units FC -> Fully connected linear output layer.

RL Taxonomy​

Drawbacks of previous methods​

  • Large state space:
    • Go: 1017010^{170}10170
    • Backgammon: 102010^{20}1020
    • Atari games: 109 to 101110^9 \text{ to } 10^{11}109 to 1011
  • Scale-up model-free based techniques for prediction and control is challenging.
  • Value function used look-up table representation
    • All states has an entry in V(s)V(s)V(s)
    • All state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) has an entry in Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a)
  • Too many state, and stat-action pair to store in memory
  • Slow learning process for each states, due to large space.
  • Each states needs to be explored sufficiently.
  • For large MDPs
    • Function approximation: Almost near optimal value.
    • Estimate value function with function approximation.
      • v^(s,w)≈vπ(s)\hat{v}(s,w) \approx v_\pi(s)v^(s,w)≈vπ​(s)
      • q^(s,a,w)≈qπ(s,a)\hat{q}(s,a,w) \approx q_\pi(s,a)q^​(s,a,w)≈qπ​(s,a)
    • Generalize from seen states to unseen states.
    • Using MC or TD learning techniques: Update parameter www.

Function Approximation​

  • A technique for estimating unknown underlying function using historical or available observations.
  • Assumption: an underlying mapping function exists
    • f(x)≈f^(x)f(x) \approx \hat{f}(x)f(x)≈f^​(x)
  • Function: x→fyx \xrightarrow{f} yxf​y

Types of Value Function Approximation​

State-value: state sss → scalar v^(s,w)\hat{v}(s,w)v^(s,w)

Action-value (s, a input): state sss and action aaa → scalar q^(s,a,w)\hat{q}(s,a,w)q^​(s,a,w)

Action-value (s input, all actions out): state sss → q^(s,a1,w),…,q^(s,am,w)\hat{q}(s,a_1,w),\ldots,\hat{q}(s,a_m,w)q^​(s,a1​,w),…,q^​(s,am​,w)

  • www is the parameter vector of the function approximator.
    • e.g. Neural Network weights

Types of Function Approximator​

  • Tabular
    • V-Table: s→v(s)s \rightarrow v(s)s→v(s)
    • Q-Table: (s,a)→q(s,a)(s,a) \rightarrow q(s,a)(s,a)→q(s,a)
  • Decision Trees, Nearest Neighbors
    • s=[speed=49,distance=10]s = [\text{speed} = 49, \text{distance} = 10]s=[speed=49,distance=10]
    • s→Decision Tree / KNN→v^(s)s \rightarrow \text{Decision Tree / KNN} \rightarrow \hat{v}(s)s→Decision Tree / KNN→v^(s)
  • Linear Function approximation
    • Linear Combination of Features
    • Values are linear function for features v^(s,w)=wTx(s)\hat{v}(s,w) = w^Tx(s)v^(s,w)=wTx(s)
    • x(s)=[speeddistancefuel]x(s) = \begin{bmatrix} \text{speed} \\ \text{distance} \\ \text{fuel} \end{bmatrix}x(s)=​speeddistancefuel​​
    • v^(s,w)=wTx(s)\hat{v}(s,w) = w^Tx(s)v^(s,w)=wTx(s)
    • v^(s,w)=w1x1(s)+⋯+wnxn(s)\hat{v}(s,w) = w_1x_1(s) + \cdots + w_n x_n(s)v^(s,w)=w1​x1​(s)+⋯+wn​xn​(s)
  • Differentiable function approximation
    • v^(s,w)\hat{v}(s,w)v^(s,w) is a differentiable function of www, can be non-linear in sss
    • e.g. Neural Network, or CNN
      • ∂v^(s,w)∂w\frac{\partial \hat{v}(s,w)}{\partial w}∂w∂v^(s,w)​
      • w←w−α∇wLw \leftarrow w - \alpha \nabla_wLw←w−α∇w​L
      • Pixels→CNNv^(s)\text{Pixels} \xrightarrow{CNN} \hat{v}(s)PixelsCNN​v^(s)

Which FA to use?​

In principle, any FA that fits the RL framework can be used.

FANotes
TabularEasy; not scalable; does not generalise
LinearRequires good features
Differentiable (better choice)Scalable; not always well understood
Neural NetworksPerforms well
Deep Neural NetworksPopular choice; performs well
  • Need training methods that are suitable for non-stationary data.

ANN​

Logistic Regression​

L(a,y)=−ylog⁡(a)−(1−y)log⁡(1−a)\mathcal{L}(a, y) = -y \log(a) - (1-y) \log(1-a)L(a,y)=−ylog(a)−(1−y)log(1−a)

  • Loss function for Logistic Regression

Gradient Descent​

Goal: Find www tht minimize J(w)J(w)J(w) or find a local minimum of J(w)J(w)J(w).

  • An iterative approach for error correction.
  • For one sample, L(a,y)=−ylog⁡(a)−(1−y)log⁡(1−a)\mathcal{L}(a, y) = -y \log(a) - (1-y) \log(1-a)L(a,y)=−ylog(a)−(1−y)log(1−a)
  • For mmm samples,

J(w,b)=1m∑i=1mL(a(i),y(i))J(w, b) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \mathcal{L}(a^{(i)}, y^{(i)})J(w,b)=m1​∑i=1m​L(a(i),y(i))

  • Find www and bbb that will minimize J(w,b)J(w, b)J(w,b)
    • min⁡w,bJ(w,b)\min_{w, b} J(w, b)minw,b​J(w,b)
    • J(w)J(w)J(w) is loss function.

w←w−α∂J(w,b)∂w,b←b−α∂J(w,b)∂bw \leftarrow w - \alpha \frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial w}, \quad b \leftarrow b - \alpha \frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial b}w←w−α∂w∂J(w,b)​,b←b−α∂b∂J(w,b)​

ΔwJ(w)=(∂J(w)∂w1,…,∂J(w)∂wn)\Delta w J(w) = \big(\frac{\partial J(w)}{\partial w_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial J(w)}{\partial w_n}\big)ΔwJ(w)=(∂w1​∂J(w)​,…,∂wn​∂J(w)​)

  • Adjust the www in the direction of the -ve gradient.
    • w=w−αΔw,b=b−αΔbw = w - \alpha \Delta w, \quad b = b - \alpha \Delta bw=w−αΔw,b=b−αΔb
    • where α\alphaα is the learning rate.
    • and, Δw=∂J(w,b)∂w,Δb=∂J(w,b)∂b\Delta w = \frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial w}, \quad \Delta b = \frac{\partial J(w, b)}{\partial b}Δw=∂w∂J(w,b)​,Δb=∂b∂J(w,b)​

ANN as a Function Approximator​

  • Need a method to estimate: Δw\Delta wΔw
  • Method to incrementally adjust and update: www
  • Representation of some aspects of RL environments as feature vector x(s)x(s)x(s)
  • Aspects can be approximated: V(s) or Q(s,a)V(s) \text{ or } Q(s, a)V(s) or Q(s,a)
    • Estimate value functions with function approximation.
    • V^(s,w)≈V(s)\hat{V}(s, \color{red}{w}\color{black}) \approx V(s)V^(s,w)≈V(s)
    • Q^(s,a,w)≈Q(s,a)\hat{Q}(s, a, \color{red}{w}\color{black}) \approx Q(s, a)Q^​(s,a,w)≈Q(s,a)
  • A mechanism to plugin MC and TD for function approximation.

Value Function Approximation for policy evaluation​

VFA: Value Function Approximation

  • vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) is given, so making it supervised.
  • v^(s,w)\hat{v}(s, w)v^(s,w) is estimated value if it follows the policy π\piπ by using ANN.
  • x→y^vsyx \rightarrow \hat{y} \quad \text{vs} \quad yx→y^​vsy (supervised learning)
  • s→v^(s,w)vsvπ(s)s \rightarrow \hat{v}(s, w) \quad \text{vs} \quad v_\pi(s)s→v^(s,w)vsvπ​(s) (Reinforcement learning)

J(w)=Eπ[(vπ(s)−v^(s,w))2] J(w) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\big(v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)\big)^2]J(w)=Eπ​[(vπ​(s)−v^(s,w))2]

  • Find www that minimizes J(w)J(w)J(w)
    • J(w)J(w)J(w): Loss function.
    • v^(s,w)\hat{v}(s, w)v^(s,w): Guess from the value function approximation.
    • vπ(s)−v^(s,w)v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)vπ​(s)−v^(s,w): Error between the true value and the estimated value.
    • Eπ[⋅]\mathbb{E}_\pi[\cdot]Eπ​[⋅]: Expected average over all states sss according to the policy π\piπ.
Δw=−12α∇wJ(w)Δw=αEπ[(vπ(s)−v^(s,w))⏟Error∇wv^(s,w)⏟Gradient]\begin{aligned} & \Delta w = -\frac{1}{2} \alpha \nabla_w J(w) \\ & \Delta w = \alpha \mathbb{E}_\pi[\underbrace{\big(v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)\big)}_{Error} \underbrace{\nabla_w \hat{v}(s, w)}_{Gradient}] \end{aligned}​Δw=−21​α∇w​J(w)Δw=αEπ​[Error(vπ​(s)−v^(s,w))​​Gradient∇w​v^(s,w)​​]​
  • Δw=\Delta w = Δw= Step size X Error X Gradient

VFA with SGD​

Δw=α(vπ(s)−v^(s,w))∇wv^(s,w) \Delta w = \alpha (v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)) \nabla_w \hat{v}(s, w)Δw=α(vπ​(s)−v^(s,w))∇w​v^(s,w)

  • Stochastic Gradient Descent sample the gradient
  • Sample a state randomly, find what vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) is, and find the estimate
    • Δw=α[Error at s×Gradient at s]\Delta w = \alpha [\text{Error at } s \times \text{Gradient at } s]Δw=α[Error at s×Gradient at s]
    • Sample sts_tst​ from π\piπ, and update www
  • Expected value update using SGD update is same as full gradient update
    • Random sampling will be eventually the same as full gradient update

Linear Value Function Approximation​

  • Represent Value function (state or action) by a linear combination of features
    • v^(s,w)=x(s)Tw=∑j=0nxj(s)wj\hat{v}(s, w) = x(s)^Tw = \sum_{j=0}^n x_j(s) w_jv^(s,w)=x(s)Tw=∑j=0n​xj​(s)wj​
  • Loss function: J(w)=Eπ[(vπ(s)−v^(s,w))2]J(w) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\big(v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)\big)^2]J(w)=Eπ​[(vπ​(s)−v^(s,w))2]

Δw=α(vπ(s)−v^(s,w))⏟Errorx(s)⏟Feature\Delta w = \alpha \underbrace{\big(v_\pi(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)\big)}_{Error} \underbrace{x(s)}_{Feature}Δw=αError(vπ​(s)−v^(s,w))​​Featurex(s)​​

  • Weight update: step size X Error X Feature value
  • SGD converges to global mininum

Incremental methods for prediction​

  • Real-world RL is not supervised, instead, it is guided by rewards.
  • No vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) is given.
  • Instead, substitute a target for vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s)

Δw=α(Gt−v^(st,w))∇wv^(st,w) \Delta w = \alpha(G_t - \hat{v}(s_t, w)) \nabla_w \hat{v}(s_t, w)Δw=α(Gt​−v^(st​,w))∇w​v^(st​,w)

  • Monte Carlo updates: target is the return GtG_tGt​

Δw=α(Rt+1+γv^(st+1,w)⏟TD Target−v^(st,w))∇wv^(st,w) \Delta w = \alpha(\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{v}(s_{t+1}, w)}_{\text{TD Target}} - \hat{v}(s_t, w)) \nabla_w \hat{v}(s_t, w)Δw=α(TD TargetRt+1​+γv^(st+1​,w)​​−v^(st​,w))∇w​v^(st​,w)

  • TD updates: use TD Target

VFA for Monte Carlo​

  • MC return GtG_tGt​ is an unbiased, noisy sample of true value vπ(st)v_\pi(s_t)vπ​(st​)
    • if Gt=3,7,4,6,5,⋯G_t = 3, 7, 4, 6, 5, \cdotsGt​=3,7,4,6,5,⋯

    • x→yx \rightarrow yx→y (supervised learning)
    • st→Gts_t \rightarrow G_tst​→Gt​ (Reinforcement learning)
  • so it learns to v^(s,w)≈Gt\hat{v}(s, w) \approx G_tv^(s,w)≈Gt​
Δw=α(Gt−v^(s,w))∇wv^(s,w)Δw=α(Gt−v^(s,w))x(s)\begin{aligned} & \Delta w = \alpha(G_t - \hat{v}(s, w)) \nabla_w \hat{v}(s, w) \\ & \Delta w = \alpha \big(G_t - \hat{v}(s, w)\big) x(s) \end{aligned}​Δw=α(Gt​−v^(s,w))∇w​v^(s,w)Δw=α(Gt​−v^(s,w))x(s)​

  • Update = Learning rate X Error X state features

VFA for TD Learning​

  • Use bootstrapping and sampling to approximate the target vπv_\pivπ​
    • Sampling: Use a sampled transition St,At,Rt+1,St+1S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​ instead of computing the full expectation over possible transitions.
    • Bootstrapping: Construct the TD target using the current estimate v^(St+1,w)\hat{v}(S_{t+1}, w)v^(St+1​,w), instead of waiting for the complete episodic return.

Rt+1+γv^(St+1,w)R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{v}(S_{t+1}, w)Rt+1​+γv^(St+1​,w)

  • TD Target is a biased sample of true value vπ(St)v_\pi(S_t)vπ​(St​)
  • Can use supervised learning on a training set of ⟨S,R⟩\langle S, R \rangle⟨S,R⟩ paris
    • ⟨S1,R2+γv^(S2,w)⟩,⟨S2,R3+γv^(S3,w)⟩,⋯ ,⟨ST−1,RT⟩\langle S_1, R_2 + \gamma \hat{v}(S_2, w) \rangle, \langle S_2, R_3 + \gamma \hat{v}(S_3, w) \rangle, \cdots, \langle S_{T-1}, R_T \rangle⟨S1​,R2​+γv^(S2​,w)⟩,⟨S2​,R3​+γv^(S3​,w)⟩,⋯,⟨ST−1​,RT​⟩

Δw=α(R+γv^(s′,w)−v^(s,w))∇wv^(s,w) \Delta w = \alpha(R + \gamma \hat{v}(s', w) - \hat{v}(s, w)) \nabla_w \hat{v}(s, w)Δw=α(R+γv^(s′,w)−v^(s,w))∇w​v^(s,w)

  • Linear VFA + TD(0) for prediction and policy evaluation
  • TD Error: δt=Rt+1+γv^(St+1,w)−v^(St,w)\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{v}(S_{t+1}, w) - \hat{v}(S_t, w)δt​=Rt+1​+γv^(St+1​,w)−v^(St​,w)
  • Δw=αδt∇wv^(St,w)\Delta w = \alpha \delta_t \nabla_w \hat{v}(S_t, w)Δw=αδt​∇w​v^(St​,w)
    • ∇wv^(s,w)=x(s)\nabla_w \hat{v}(s, w) = x(s)∇w​v^(s,w)=x(s)
    • Δw=αδtx(s)\Delta w = \alpha \delta_t x(s)Δw=αδt​x(s)
    • w←w−αδtx(s)w \leftarrow w - \alpha \delta_t x(s)w←w−αδt​x(s)
Initialize w=0Loop:Initialize sSample transition (s,a,r,s′) using policy πWeight update: w←w−α(R+γv^(s′,w)−v^(s,w))x(s)\begin{aligned} & \text{Initialize } w = 0 \\ & Loop: \\ & \quad \text{Initialize } s \\ & \quad \text{Sample transition } (s, a, r, s') \text{ using policy } \pi \\ & \quad \text{Weight update: } \quad w \leftarrow w - \alpha(R + \gamma \hat{v}(s', w) - \hat{v}(s, w))x(s) \\ & \end{aligned}​Initialize w=0Loop:Initialize sSample transition (s,a,r,s′) using policy πWeight update: w←w−α(R+γv^(s′,w)−v^(s,w))x(s)​

Overall​

  • Linear VFA: v^(s,w)=wTx(s)\hat{v}(s, w) = w^Tx(s)v^(s,w)=wTx(s)
  • MC Target = GtG_tGt​
  • TD Target = Rt+1+γv^(s′,w)R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{v}(s', w)Rt+1​+γv^(s′,w)
  • MC: w←w+α(Gt−v^(s,w))x(s)w \leftarrow w + \alpha(G_t - \hat{v}(s, w)) x(s)w←w+α(Gt​−v^(s,w))x(s)

Temporal-Difference Learning​

Updates a guess towards a guess.

  • Model-free: No MDP Dynamics or Rewards
  • Learns directly from episodes of experience.
  • Bootstrapping: Estimate value function using estimated value from incomplete episodes.
    • Update estimate using another estimate.
  • Updates the estimate of VVV immediately after each step.
  • Combines Monte Carlo and Dynamic Programming (Bootstrapping idea).

MC​

V(St)=V(St)+α[Gt⏟Goal−V(St)⏟Previous estimate]V(S_t) = V(S_t) + \alpha [\underbrace{G_t}_{\text{Goal}} - \underbrace{V(S_t)}_{\text{Previous estimate}} ]V(St​)=V(St​)+α[GoalGt​​​−Previous estimateV(St​)​​]

  • Update V(St)V(S_t)V(St​) towards the actual return.
  • α=1n\alpha = \frac{1}{n}α=n1​: Every-visit MC.
    • gives equal weight to all past samples in the arithmetic mean.
  • Fixed α>1n\alpha > \frac{1}{n}α>n1​: gives more weight to recent experience and reduces the influence of older episodes faster.
    • α=0.1,V(S)=10\alpha = 0.1, \quad V(S) = 10α=0.1,V(S)=10
    • V(S)←10+0.1(20−10)=11V(S) \leftarrow 10 + 0.1 (20 - 10) = 11V(S)←10+0.1(20−10)=11
    • V(S)←11+0.1(30−11)=12.9V(S) \leftarrow 11 + 0.1 (30 - 11) = 12.9V(S)←11+0.1(30−11)=12.9
    • Move 10% of the way towards the new value.

One-Step Bootstrapping​

TD(0)→TD(λ)→TD(1)≈MC\text{TD}(0) \rightarrow \text{TD}(\lambda) \rightarrow \text{TD}(1) \approx \text{MC}TD(0)→TD(λ)→TD(1)≈MC

  • λ\lambdaλ controls how much longer-term return information is used in the TD update.
    • It controls how far into the future TD learns from.
  • λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0: uses one-step bootstrapping, corresponding to TD(0).
  • As λ\lambdaλ increases, rewards further into the future have more influence on the update.
  • λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1: approaches the Monte Carlo return in episodic tasks.

V(St)=V(St)+α[Rt+1+γV(St+1)⏟TD target−V(St)⏟TD Error]V(S_t) = V(S_t) + \alpha [\underbrace{\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - V(S_t)}_{\text{TD Error}} ]V(St​)=V(St​)+α[TD ErrorTD targetRt+1​+γV(St+1​)​​−V(St​)​​]

  • Only one immediate reward is used Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​.
  • Everything after that is replaced by the current guess V(St+1)V(S_{t+1})V(St+1​) instead of actual future rewards.
  • It uses actual reward for the first step and the estimated value/guess for the rest.
MC
Sₜ ──Rₜ₊₁──> Sₜ₊₁ ──Rₜ₊₂──> ... ──> Terminal
│                                        │
└────────── episode 끝까지 기다림 ────────┘
                   ↓
               actual Gₜ
                   ↓
              V(Sₜ) update


TD(0)
Sₜ ──Rₜ₊₁──> Sₜ₊₁ ── ? ──> ...
│              │
│              └─ current V(Sₜ₊₁)
│
└── Rₜ₊₁ + γV(Sₜ₊₁)로 즉시 V(Sₜ) update

TD(0) Algorithm​

Loop for each episode:InitializeSLoop for each step of the episode:A←action given by policyπTake actionA,observeR,S′V(S)←V(S)+α[R+γV(S′)−V(S)]S←S′UntilS is terminal\begin{aligned} &\text{Loop for each episode:} \\ &\quad \text{Initialize} \quad S \\ &\quad \text{Loop for each step of the episode:} \\ &\quad \quad A \leftarrow \text{action given by policy} \quad \pi \\ &\quad \quad \text{Take action} \quad A, \quad \text{observe} \quad R, \quad S' \\ &\quad \quad V(S) \leftarrow V(S) + \alpha [R + \gamma V(S') - V(S)] \\ &\quad \quad S \leftarrow S' \\ &\quad \text{Until} \quad S \text{ is terminal} \\ \end{aligned} ​Loop for each episode:InitializeSLoop for each step of the episode:A←action given by policyπTake actionA,observeR,S′V(S)←V(S)+α[R+γV(S′)−V(S)]S←S′UntilS is terminal​
  • No need to wait until the end of the episode to update the value function.

MC vs. TD​

AspectMonte Carlo (MC)Temporal-Difference (TD)
Learning sequenceLearns from complete episodesLearns from incomplete episodes
TargetActual return GtG_tGt​Estimated return using bootstrapping
Update timingAfter the episode endsBefore the episode ends / step by step
Future informationUses actual future rewardsUses observed reward(s) + estimated future value
BootstrappingNoYes
BiasUnbiasedBiased
VarianceHighLow
EnvironmentEpisodic / terminating environmentsAlso works in continuing / non-terminating environments
Practical speedSlower updatesFaster updates in practice

  • In practice, TD is faster than MC because it can learn from incomplete episodes.

  • MC: Full sampled path to the end.
  • TD: Just one real step.
  • DP: Every branch, weighted by probability, no sampling.

SARSA​

St,At,Rt+1,St+1,At+1S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​,At+1​

  • Follows generalized Policy Iteration.
    • Policy Evaluation: TD Policy Evaluation Q≈qπQ \approx q_\piQ≈qπ​
    • Policy Improvement: ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy policy improvement, allowing exploration.
    • Update happens after every time step.
  • Use TD methods for evaluation. Q(S,A)Q(S, A)Q(S,A)
  • TD Evaluation + ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy Policy Improvement = SARSA

Q(St,At)=Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γQ(St+1,At+1)⏟TD target−Q(St,At)]Q(S_t, A_t) = Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha [\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - Q(S_t, A_t)]Q(St​,At​)=Q(St​,At​)+α[TD targetRt+1​+γQ(St+1​,At+1​)​​−Q(St​,At​)]

  • (St,At,Rt+1,St+1,At+1)(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})(St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​,At+1​): transition from one state-action pair to the next.
  • The process repeatedly alternates between improving QQQ and improving the policy.
  • The estimates gradually move toward the optimal action-value function q∗q_*q∗​ and the optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​.
  • Unlike classical policy iteration, SARSA does not need to complete policy evaluation before improving the policy.

SARSA Example​

  • Q(St,At)=10Q(S_t,A_t)=10Q(St​,At​)=10
  • Rt+1=2R_{t+1}=2Rt+1​=2
  • γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9
  • α=0.5\alpha=0.5α=0.5
  • Q(St+1,At+1)=8Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1})=8Q(St+1​,At+1​)=8
  • TD Target =2+0.9(8)=9.2=2+0.9(8)=9.2=2+0.9(8)=9.2
  • TD Error =9.2−10=−0.8=9.2-10=-0.8=9.2−10=−0.8
  • Updated Q(St,At)=10+0.5(−0.8)=9.6Q(S_t,A_t)=10+0.5(-0.8)=9.6Q(St​,At​)=10+0.5(−0.8)=9.6

SARSA Algorithm​

Loop for each episode:InitializeSChooseAt from St using policy π derived from QLoop for each step of the episode:Take actionAt+1,observeRt+1,St+1Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γQ(St+1,At+1)−Q(St,At)]St←St+1At←At+1UntilS is terminal\begin{aligned} &\text{Loop for each episode:} \\ &\quad \text{Initialize} \quad S \\ &\quad \text{Choose} A_t \text{ from } S_t \text{ using policy } \pi \text{ derived from } Q\\ &\quad \text{Loop for each step of the episode:} \\ &\quad \quad \text{Take action} \quad A_{t+1}, \quad \text{observe} \quad R_{t+1}, \quad S_{t+1} \\ &\quad \quad Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha [R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) - Q(S_t, A_t)] \\ &\quad \quad S_t \leftarrow S_{t+1} \\ &\quad \quad A_t \leftarrow A_{t+1} \\ &\quad \text{Until} \quad S \text{ is terminal} \\ \end{aligned}​Loop for each episode:InitializeSChooseAt​ from St​ using policy π derived from QLoop for each step of the episode:Take actionAt+1​,observeRt+1​,St+1​Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γQ(St+1​,At+1​)−Q(St​,At​)]St​←St+1​At​←At+1​UntilS is terminal​
  • As SARSA learns, each episode is completed faster.
  • As the Q-values improve, the agent learns better actions for each state and reaches the goal using fewer steps.

Q-Learning​

  • On-policy: SARSA, behavior policy is the same as the target policy.
  • Off-policy: Q-Learning, behavior policy is different from the target policy. Q(S,A)Q(S, A)Q(S,A)
  • Update Q(St,At)Q(S_t, A_t)Q(St​,At​) toward the value of the alternative, best action.

Q(St,At)=Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γmax⁡aQ(St+1,a)⏟TD target−Q(St,At)] Q(S_t, A_t) = Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha [\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a} Q(S_{t+1}, a)}_{\text{TD target}} - Q(S_t, A_t)]Q(St​,At​)=Q(St​,At​)+α[TD targetRt+1​+γamax​Q(St+1​,a)​​−Q(St​,At​)]

  • The Actual next action is replaced by the Best possible action.

Q-Learning Algorithm​

Loop for each episode:InitializeSLoop for each step of the episode:At fromSt using policy π derived from QTake actionAt+1,observeRt+1,St+1Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γmax⁡aQ(St+1,a)−Q(St,At)]St←St+1UntilS is terminal\begin{aligned} &\text{Loop for each episode:} \\ &\quad \text{Initialize} \quad S \\ &\quad \text{Loop for each step of the episode:} \\ &\quad \quad A_t \text{ from} S_t \text{ using policy } \pi \text{ derived from } Q\\ &\quad \quad \text{Take action} \quad A_{t+1}, \quad \text{observe} \quad R_{t+1}, \quad S_{t+1} \\ &\quad \quad Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha [R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a} Q(S_{t+1}, a) - Q(S_t, A_t)] \\ &\quad \quad S_t \leftarrow S_{t+1} \\ &\quad \text{Until} \quad S \text{ is terminal} \\ \end{aligned}​Loop for each episode:InitializeSLoop for each step of the episode:At​ fromSt​ using policy π derived from QTake actionAt+1​,observeRt+1​,St+1​Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γamax​Q(St+1​,a)−Q(St​,At​)]St​←St+1​UntilS is terminal​

Cliff Walking​

  • SARSA (on-policy) accounts for ε-greedy exploration near the cliff and learns the safer route.
  • Q-Learning (off-policy) learns the optimal route.
    • but occasionally falls off the cliff during exploration, hurting its online performance

Known MDP vs Unknown MDP​

AspectKnown MDPUnknown MDP
Environment Knowledge (P,RP, RP,R)Full knowledge of state transition dynamics PPP and reward function RRRPPP and RRR are unknown; agent must explore the environment
Problem ApproachWell-defined optimization problem →\rightarrow→ Pure planning via computationTrial-and-error interaction →\rightarrow→ Must learn and optimize simultaneously
Primary GoalDirectly compute the optimal policy (π∗\pi_*π∗​)Learn and optimize policies without prior model knowledge
Representative MethodsValue Iteration, Policy Iteration (Dynamic Programming)Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, SARSA (Reinforcement Learning)
ParadigmModel-based (Planning)Model-free (Reinforcement Learning)

Model-based vs Model-free​

AspectModel-Based LearningModel-Free Learning
Model Access (P,RP, RP,R)Has full access to transition dynamics PPP and reward function RRRNo access to environment dynamics (PPP and RRR are unknown)
Optimization ApproachDirect mathematical computation and planning using the known modelDirect learning and trial-and-error optimization through interaction
Estimation SourceComputes values and optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​ via dynamic programming equationsEstimates vπ,qπv_\pi, q_\pivπ​,qπ​, and π∗\pi_*π∗​ directly from sampled experience
Computation vs. SamplingPure computation / Planning (requires no real-time environment sampling)Sample-based learning (requires trajectories / episodic experience)
Typical MethodsPolicy Iteration, Value Iteration (DP)Monte Carlo Methods, TD Learning, Q-Learning, SARSA

Monte Carlo Methods​

  • A Computational technique that uses random sampling and statistical methods to solve complex problems and estimate numerical results.
    • Named after the Monte Carlo Casino in Monaco.
    • It means Estimate an unknown quantity by sampling, and averaging what you observe.
  • Used fo any estimation method whose operation involves a significant random component.
  • Used in mathematics, physics, engineering, finance, computer science, etc.
  • It is particularly valuable when an analytical solution is difficult or impossible to obtain.

Estimating π\piπ by Sampling (Monte Carlo Simulation)​

  • Mechanism:
    • Generate uniform random points (x,y)∈[−1,1]×[−1,1](x, y) \in [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1](x,y)∈[−1,1]×[−1,1].
    • Count points falling inside the unit circle (x2+y2≤1x^2 + y^2 \le 1x2+y2≤1).
    • Estimate π\piπ via area proportions:
AreacircleAreasquare=π4π≈4×#points inside circle#total points\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{Area}_{circle}}{\text{Area}_{square}} = \frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \pi \approx 4 \times \frac{\text{\#points inside circle}}{\text{\#total points}} \end{aligned}Areasquare​Areacircle​​=4π​​π≈4×#total points#points inside circle​​
  • Empirical Validation:
    • Total samples (nnn): 300030003000 points
    • Estimated value: π=3.1386666666666665\pi = 3.1386666666666665π=3.1386666666666665
    • Relative error: −0.0931%-0.0931\%−0.0931% from true value (≈3.14159265\approx 3.14159265≈3.14159265)

Monte Carlo Prediction​

vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]≈1N∑i=1N(s)G(i)v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t | S_t = s] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N(s)} G^{(i)}vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]≈N1​∑i=1N(s)​G(i)

  • 1N∑i=1N(s)G(i)\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N(s)} G^{(i)}N1​∑i=1N(s)​G(i): Mean of the returns/rewards
  • Model-Free Learning: Operates without prior knowledge of transition dynamics PPP or reward function RRR.
  • Learning from Complete Episodes: Learns state-value functions vπv_\pivπ​ exclusively from full trajectories under policy π\piπ. Only works for episodic tasks where termination at step TTT is guaranteed.
  • No Bootstrapping: Does not update estimates using other value estimates v(s′)v(s')v(s′); instead, updates rely solely on actual empirical returns observed at the end of the episode.
  • Empirical Mean Returns: The value of state sss is estimated by the sample average of all observed returns starting from sss:

An Episode of Experience & Return Formulation​

  • Trajectory Structure: S0→A0,R1S1→A1,R2S2⋯→AT−1,RTSTS_0 \xrightarrow{A_0, R_1} S_1 \xrightarrow{A_1, R_2} S_2 \dots \xrightarrow{A_{T-1}, R_T} S_TS0​A0​,R1​​S1​A1​,R2​​S2​⋯AT−1​,RT​​ST​
  • Discounted Return (GtG_tGt​): Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯+γT−t−1RTG_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \dots + \gamma^{T-t-1} R_TGt​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯+γT−t−1RT​
  • Discount Factor (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1): For episodic tasks with terminal-only rewards (such as Blackjack), setting γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 is standard practice because the episode length is finite.

First-Visit Monte Carlo​

  • First-Visit MC estimates the value function V(s)V(s)V(s) by averaging returns following only the first occurrence of state sss within each sampled episode.

    • For each time step ttt where state sss appears in episode iii:
      • N(s)←N(s)+1N(s) \leftarrow N(s) + 1N(s)←N(s)+1 (Increment counter for total visits)
      • G(s)←G(s)+Gi,tG(s) \leftarrow G(s) + G_{i,t}G(s)←G(s)+Gi,t​ (Increment total return)

Incremental Mean​

μk=1k∑j=1kxj\mu_k = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} x_jμk​=k1​∑j=1k​xj​

μk+1=1k+1∑j=1k+1xj=1k+1(∑j=1kxj+xk+1)=1k+1(kμk+xk+1)=μk+1k+1(xk+1−μk)\begin{aligned} \mu_{k+1} &= \frac{1}{k+1} \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} x_j \\ &= \frac{1}{k+1} \left( \sum_{j=1}^{k} x_j + x_{k+1} \right) \\ &= \frac{1}{k+1} \left( k \mu_k + x_{k+1} \right) \\ &= \mu_k + \frac{1}{k+1} (x_{k+1} - \mu_k) \end{aligned}μk+1​​=k+11​j=1∑k+1​xj​=k+11​(j=1∑k​xj​+xk+1​)=k+11​(kμk​+xk+1​)=μk​+k+11​(xk+1​−μk​)​
  • New estimate = Old estimate + step-size * (new sample - old estimate).
  • Memory efficient: Only need to store the old estimate (μk\mu_kμk​) and the number of visits (kkk).

Incremental Monte Carlo​

  • Updates the value function V(s)V(s)V(s) incrementally after each trajectory without requiring memory to store individual past returns.
  • Algorithmic Flow:
    • Initialize N(s)←0N(s) \leftarrow 0N(s)←0 and V(s)←0V(s) \leftarrow 0V(s)←0 for all s∈Ss \in Ss∈S.
    • Episode sampling: Execute episode iii under policy π\piπ and compute returns Gi,t=∑k=t+1Tiγk−t−1RkG_{i,t} = \sum_{k=t+1}^{T_i} \gamma^{k-t-1} R_{k}Gi,t​=∑k=t+1Ti​​γk−t−1Rk​.
    • Incremental update: For each visited state sss at time step ttt:
      • N(s)←N(s)+1N(s) \leftarrow N(s) + 1N(s)←N(s)+1 (Increment counter for total visits)
      • V(s)←V(s)+α(Gi,t−V(s))V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha (G_{i,t} - V(s))V(s)←V(s)+α(Gi,t​−V(s)) (Update the value by mean return)
      • Where Gi,t−V(s)G_{i,t} - V(s)Gi,t​−V(s) represents the temporal difference (TD) error between the sampled return target and the current estimate.
  • Choice step size α\alphaα
    • α=1N(s)\alpha = \frac{1}{N(s)}α=N(s)1​: Replicates the exact empirical sample-average of Every-Visit MC where all observed samples receive equal weight.
    • α=constant\alpha = \text{constant}α=constant: Implements an exponential recency-weighted running average that decays outdated experience, making it suited for non-stationary environments where MDP dynamics change over time.
  • Cons:
    • Requires a significant number of episodes to converge to the true value function.
    • Requires to terminate the episode.

Model-free Control​

  • The MDP model is unknown, or too large/complex to use directly.
  • But experience can be sampled.
  • Applications:
    • Robo soccer
    • Autonomous vehicles
    • Robotics
    • Game playing
    • Recommender systems
    • Finance & portfolio management

On-Policy vs Off-Policy​

DimensionOn-Policy LearningOff-Policy Learning
DefinitionEvaluates and improves the exact same policy currently used to generate action decisionsEvaluates/improves a target policy (π\piπ) while behaving via a different behavior policy (bbb)
Data GenerationTrajectories must be generated by the current active policy π\piπTrajectories can come from exploratory policies, historical logs, or human demonstrations
Exploration Trade-offMust balance exploration directly within the target policy (e.g., ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy)Separates exploration (behavior policy) from exploitation/optimality (target policy)
Representative AlgorithmsGLIE Monte Carlo Control, SARSAQ-Learning, Deep Q-Networks (DQN)

General Policy Iteration​

  • Alternates between Policy Evaluation (V≈vπV \approx v_\piV≈vπ​ or Q≈qπQ \approx q_\piQ≈qπ​) and Policy Improvement (π←greedy\pi \leftarrow \text{greedy}π←greedy).
  • This interplay drives the system asymptotically toward the optimal pair (v∗,π∗)(v_*, \pi_*)(v∗​,π∗​) or (q∗,π∗)(q_*, \pi_*)(q∗​,π∗​).

π′(s)=argmaxa∈A(R(s,a)+γ∑s′∈SP(s′∣s,a)V(s′))\pi'(s) = \text{argmax}_{a \in A} \big( \mathcal{R}(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in S} \mathcal{P}(s' | s, a) V(s') \big)π′(s)=argmaxa∈A​(R(s,a)+γ∑s′∈S​P(s′∣s,a)V(s′))

  • Why V(s)V(s)V(s) Fails in Model-Free Settings:
    • Finding the maximizing action over V(s)V(s)V(s) strictly requires the transition model P(s′∣s,a)P(s' \mid s, a)P(s′∣s,a) and reward function R(s,a)R(s, a)R(s,a).
    • In Model-Free RL, these dynamics are unavailable; hence, V(s)V(s)V(s) alone cannot guide policy updates without an explicit environment model.

π′(s)=argmaxa∈AQ(s,a)\pi'(s) = \text{argmax}_{a \in A}Q(s,a)π′(s)=argmaxa∈A​Q(s,a)

  • Model-Free Advantage:
    • By estimating Q(s,a)Q(s, a)Q(s,a) directly through sample episodes, policy improvement requires no knowledge of PPP or RRR.
    • This fundamental shift makes Q(s,a)Q(s, a)Q(s,a) estimation the standard paradigm for Model-Free Control (Monte Carlo Control, SARSA, Q-Learning).
V(s)V(s)V(s)Q(s,a)Q(s, a)Q(s,a)
QuestionHow good is this state?How good is this action in this state?
Includes Action?NoYes
Policy EvaluationVery suitableSlightly more difficult

Model-Free ControlInconvenientVery suitable

  • This is why MC Control estimates qπ(s,a)q_\pi(s,a)qπ​(s,a), not vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s).

Exploration Problem​

a=arg⁡max⁡aQ(s,a)a = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)a=argamax​Q(s,a)
  • A greedy agent always chooses the action with the highest current estimated value.
  • But what if the current Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) estimates are inaccurate?

Mystery Box Example​

Initially,

Q(red)=0,Q(blue)=0Q(\text{red}) = 0, \qquad Q(\text{blue}) = 0Q(red)=0,Q(blue)=0

  1. Open the red box:
    R=0→Q(red)=0R = 0 \rightarrow Q(\text{red}) = 0R=0→Q(red)=0

  2. Open the blue box:
    R=+1→Q(blue)=1R = +1 \rightarrow Q(\text{blue}) = 1R=+1→Q(blue)=1

  3. Keep opening the blue box:
    R=+1,+3,+2,…→Q(blue)≈2R = +1, +3, +2, \ldots \rightarrow Q(\text{blue}) \approx 2R=+1,+3,+2,…→Q(blue)≈2

  4. A purely greedy agent now keeps choosing the blue box because
    Q(blue)>Q(red)Q(\text{blue}) > Q(\text{red})Q(blue)>Q(red).

  5. However, the red box may actually be better. For example,
    E[R∣red]=5\mathbb{E}[R \mid \text{red}] = 5E[R∣red]=5.

    The agent does not know this because it sampled the red box only once.

Exploitation vs. Exploration​

  • Exploitation: Choose the action that currently has the highest estimated value.
  • Exploration: Try less-sampled or unfamiliar actions to discover whether they may actually be better.
  • In this example, the agent should occasionally explore the red box because it has not been sampled enough to confidently conclude that it is worse.

ϵ\epsilonϵ-Greedy Exploration​

π(a∣s)={greedy action with high probabilityrandom action with probability ϵ\pi(a|s) = \begin{cases} \text{greedy action \quad with high probability} \\ \text{random action \quad with probability $\epsilon$} \\ \end{cases}π(a∣s)={greedy action with high probabilityrandom action with probability ϵ​
  • if ϵ=0.1\epsilon = 0.1ϵ=0.1, then the agent will choose the greedy action with probability 0.90.90.9 (Exploitation)
  • And the random action with probability 0.10.10.1 (Exploration).
  • Policy Improvement Theorem:
    • for any ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy policy π\piπ
    • The ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy policy π′\pi'π′ is as good or better than the original policy π\piπ: vπ′(s)≥vπ(s)v_{\pi'}(s) \geq v_{\pi}(s)vπ′​(s)≥vπ​(s)

Monte Carlo Control​

  • Traditional Policy Iteration:
    • Fix the policy π\piπ.
    • Evaluate the current policy until QQQ is sufficiently close to qπ(s,a)q_\pi(s,a)qπ​(s,a).
    • Improve the policy using the estimated action values.
    • Repeat policy evaluation and policy improvement.
  • Monte Carlo Control:
    • Perform MC Policy Evaluation after every episode.
    • Improve the policy using ϵ\epsilonϵ-greedy after every episode.
    • Q1→π1=ϵ-greedy(Q1)Q_1 \rightarrow \pi_1 = \epsilon\text{-greedy}(Q_1)Q1​→π1​=ϵ-greedy(Q1​)
    • Q2→π2=ϵ-greedy(Q2)Q_2 \rightarrow \pi_2 = \epsilon\text{-greedy}(Q_2)Q2​→π2​=ϵ-greedy(Q2​)
    • ⋯\cdots⋯
    • Eventually approaches (q∗,π∗)(q_*, \pi_*)(q∗​,π∗​) under appropriate convergence conditions.

Evaluate a little→Improve→Evaluate a little→Improve→⋯\text{Evaluate a little} \rightarrow \text{Improve} \rightarrow \text{Evaluate a little} \rightarrow \text{Improve} \rightarrow \cdotsEvaluate a little→Improve→Evaluate a little→Improve→⋯

GLIE​

Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration

  1. lim⁡k→∞Nk(s,a)=∞\lim_{k \to \infty} N_k(s,a) = \inftylimk→∞​Nk​(s,a)=∞
  2. lim⁡k→∞πk(a∣s)=1(a=arg max⁡a′∈AQk(s,a′))\lim_{k \to \infty} \pi_k(a|s) = 1(a = \argmax_{a' \in A} Q_k(s,a'))limk→∞​πk​(a∣s)=1(a=argmaxa′∈A​Qk​(s,a′))
  • Explore enough early -> Explore less over time -> Eventually greedy.
    • Nk(s,a)N_k(s,a)Nk​(s,a): How many times the state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) has been visited in the kkk-th episode.
    • πk→greedy(Qk)\pi_k \rightarrow \text{greedy}(Q_k)πk​→greedy(Qk​)
  • Infinite exploration first, greedy behavior in the limit.

GILE Monte Carlo Control​

  • Algorithm flow:
    • Run episode k={S0,A0,R1,…,ST}k = \{S_0, A_0, R_1, \dots, S_{T}\}k={S0​,A0​,R1​,…,ST​} with policy πk\pi_kπk​.
    • For each state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) in the episode:
      • Nk(s,a)←Nk(s,a)+1N_k(s,a) \leftarrow N_k(s,a) + 1Nk​(s,a)←Nk​(s,a)+1
      • Qk(s,a)←Qk(s,a)+1Nk(s,a)(Gk−Qk(s,a))Q_k(s,a) \leftarrow Q_k(s,a) + \frac{1}{N_k(s,a)} (G_k - Q_k(s,a))Qk​(s,a)←Qk​(s,a)+Nk​(s,a)1​(Gk​−Qk​(s,a))
    • Improve the policy based on the new QQQ value.
      • ϵ←1k\epsilon \leftarrow \frac{1}{k}ϵ←k1​
      • π←ϵ-greedy(Q)\pi \leftarrow \epsilon\text{-greedy}(Q)π←ϵ-greedy(Q)
    • Repeat until convergence.
  • old estimate + step-size * (new sample - old estimate).
    • old estimate = Q(St,At)Q(S_t, A_t)Q(St​,At​)
    • new sample = GtG_tGt​
    • step-size = 1Nk(s,a)\frac{1}{N_k(s,a)}Nk​(s,a)1​
  • Run Episode → Update Q → Reduce ϵ\epsilonϵ → Improve Policy

DP vs MC​

  • Dynamic Programming:
    • Model-based
    • Bootstrapping: Updating a value estimate using another estimated value instead of waiting for the final outcome.
    • Lower variance
  • Monte Carlo:
    • Model-free
    • No bootstrapping: It uses rewards that actually occurred, not an estimated value of the next state.
    • Uses complete sampled returns
    • Requires episodic tasks
    • Higher variance

MDP​

(S,A,P,R,γ)(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, \gamma)(S,A,P,R,γ)

  • At each time step ttt, the agent observes state St∈SS_t \in \mathcal{S}St​∈S and chooses action At∈AA_t \in \mathcal{A}At​∈A
  • Receives reward Rt+1∈RR_{t+1} \in \mathcal{R}Rt+1​∈R
  • Transitions to a new state St+1S_{t+1}St+1​

Transition Dynamics​

Transition Probability

  • How the environment responds to an action, independent of the agent's policy
  • Policy: Whether to brake or accelerate when the traffic light is yellow.
  • Transition Dynamics: How much the car decelerates after braking, and what the resulting next state is.

P(s′∣s,a)=P(St+1=s′∣St=s,At=a)P(s'|s,a) = P(S_{t+1} = s'|S_t = s, A_t = a)P(s′∣s,a)=P(St+1​=s′∣St​=s,At​=a)

Policy​

  • A policy is the agent’s rule for choosing actions.
  • It tells the agent what action to take in a given state.
  • It defines agent's behavior.

Deterministic Policy:π(s)=a\text{Deterministic Policy}: \pi(s) = aDeterministic Policy:π(s)=a

  • Direct mapping, and no randomness
  • All probability on one action

Stochastic Policy:π(a∣s)=P(At=a∣St=s)\text{Stochastic Policy}: \pi(a|s) = P(A_t = a | S_t = s)Stochastic Policy:π(a∣s)=P(At​=a∣St​=s)

  • A probability distribution over actions.
  • More general, all four Bellman Equations are stochastic, use π(a∣s)\pi(a|s)π(a∣s) to represent the policy.
  • Policy is what the agent controls.

Value Functions​

vπ(s)=Eπ[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) | S_t = s]vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]

  • How good is this state?
  • Eπ[Gt∣St=s]\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t | S_t = s]Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]

qπ(s,a)=Eπ[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s,At=a]q_\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) | S_t = s, A_t = a]qπ​(s,a)=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s,At​=a]

  • How good is this action in this state?
  • Eπ[Gt∣St=s,At=a]\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t | S_t = s, A_t = a]Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s,At​=a]

vπ(s)=∑a∈Aπ(a∣s)qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a|s) q_\pi(s,a)vπ​(s)=∑a∈A​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a)

  • The average value of the actions, weighted by the probability of choosing each action.
    • a1a_1a1​ is brake
    • a2a_2a2​ is accelerate
    • vπ(s)=0.8∗10+0.2∗20=10v_\pi(s) = 0.8 * 10 + 0.2 * 20 = 10vπ​(s)=0.8∗10+0.2∗20=10

  • The value of taking action aaa in state sss: the immediate reward plus the discounted expected value of the possible next states.

Four Types of Bellman Equations​

vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)qπ(s,a)qπ(s,a)=R(s,a)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s,a)vπ(s′)vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)[R(s,a)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s,a)vπ(s′)]qπ(s,a)=R(s,a)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s,a)∑a′π(a′∣s′)qπ(s′,a′)\begin{aligned} &v_\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a|s) q_\pi(s,a) \\ &q_\pi(s,a) = \mathcal{R}(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) v_\pi(s') \\ &v_\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a|s) \left[ \mathcal{R}(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) v_\pi(s') \right] \\ &q_\pi(s,a) = \mathcal{R}(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) \sum_{a'} \pi(a'|s') q_\pi(s',a') \end{aligned}​vπ​(s)=a∑​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a)qπ​(s,a)=R(s,a)+γs′∑​P(s′∣s,a)vπ​(s′)vπ​(s)=a∑​π(a∣s)[R(s,a)+γs′∑​P(s′∣s,a)vπ​(s′)]qπ​(s,a)=R(s,a)+γs′∑​P(s′∣s,a)a′∑​π(a′∣s′)qπ​(s′,a′)​
  • Evaluate a state: vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s)

Dynamic Programming​

Optimization method for sequential problem

  • Dynamic: Sequential or Temporal component
  • Programming: Optimizing a program or policy
  • Sub Problem
  • Optimal Solution

Prediction and Control​

  • Prediction: Evaluate a given policy vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s)
  • Control: Find the optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​

Policy Improvement​

  • π→vπ→π′\pi \to v_\pi \to \pi'π→vπ​→π′
  • π′=greedy(vπ)\pi' = \text{greedy}(v_\pi)π′=greedy(vπ​)
  • Evaluate current policy, Improve it greedily, then get a better policy

Modified Policy Iteration​

  • Policy iteration can be computationally expensive
  • MPI: cut off the policy evaluation after a few iterations kkk then step to policy improvement.
    • k=1⇒Value iterationk = 1 \Rightarrow \text{Value iteration}k=1⇒Value iteration
    • k=3,4⇒Modified Policy iterationk = 3,4 \Rightarrow \text{Modified Policy iteration}k=3,4⇒Modified Policy iteration
    • kis large enough⇒Policy iterationk \quad \text{is large enough} \Rightarrow \text{Policy iteration}kis large enough⇒Policy iteration

Poisson Distribution Formulation​

P(X=n)=λne−λn!P(X = n) = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda}}{n!}P(X=n)=n!λne−λ​

  • How many times an event occurs within a fixed interval of time (or space) when we only know the long-term average rate (λ\lambdaλ).
  • nnn: The actual number of requests or returns (n∈{0,1,2,…}n \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}n∈{0,1,2,…})
  • λ\lambdaλ: The expected/average number of requests or returns
  • eee: Euler's number (2.71828)
  • n!n!n!: Factorial of nnn

Deterministic Value Iteration​

v∗(s)=max⁡a(R(s,a)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s,a)v∗(s′))v_*(s) = \max_{a} \left( \mathcal{R}(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) v_*(s') \right)v∗​(s)=maxa​(R(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)v∗​(s′))

  • If solutions to sub-problems v∗(s′)v_*(s')v∗​(s′) are known, the optimal value v∗(s)v_*(s)v∗​(s) for the current state can be computed directly.
  • Value signals propagate backwards across the state space from states with terminal rewards.

Value Iteration​

vk+1(s)=max⁡a(R(s,a)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s,a)vk(s′))v_{k+1}(s) = \max_{a} \left( \mathcal{R}(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) v_k(s') \right)vk+1​(s)=maxa​(R(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)vk​(s′))

  • Infinite (∞\infty∞) iterations are required to converge exactly to v∗v_*v∗​.
  • In practical implementations, iteration terminates when the maximum value change between iterations is less than a small threshold θ\thetaθ.
