Efficiency of DP​

  • Strengths:
    • A foundational and efficient framework widely used for solving MDPs.
    • Mathematically guaranteed to converge to an optimal policy in polynomial time in terms of the number of states and actions.
    • Exponentially faster than exhaustive direct search across the policy space (∣A∣∣S∣|A|^{|S|}∣A∣∣S∣).
  • Limitations:
    • Can become computationally impractical for extremely large or complex environments.
    • Curse of Dimensionality: As the number of state variables (dimensions) increases, the total state space size (∣S∣|S|∣S∣) expands exponentially, leading to severe computational and memory bottlenecks.

Asynchronous Dynamic Programming​

  • Comparison with Synchronous Methods: Standard DP methods sweep through the entire state space systematically in every iteration. Asynchronous DP backs up individual states independently in arbitrary order.
  • In-place Value Updates: Directly overwrites values in a single memory array, allowing immediate propagation of newly updated state values to subsequent calculations.
  • Computational Gain & Convergence:
    • Significantly reduces computation by avoiding exhaustive full-state sweeps.
    • Guaranteed to converge to the optimal value function v∗v_*v∗​, provided that all states continue to be selected and updated indefinitely.

Real-Time Dynamic Programming (RTDP)​

  • Interaction-Driven Online Updates: Solves sub-problems on-the-fly by focusing updates specifically on states that are directly relevant to the agent's current trajectory.
  • Target Applications: Large-scale environments where full state-space iteration is intractable (e.g., robotics, autonomous control systems, game AI).
  • Core Characteristics:
    • Online Decision Making: Makes and refines decisions while operating directly in the environment.
    • Lazy Evaluation: Computes values only for visited or critical state subsets rather than unvisited distant states.
    • Adaptive Exploration: Guides search toward high-reward trajectories through active interaction.
    • Approximate MDP Solution: Yields near-optimal policies for relevant regions without solving the global MDP.

Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP)​

  • Motivation: Addresses the curse of dimensionality where tabular representation of states and exact value computation become computationally infeasible.
  • Function Approximation Methods: Parameterizes and estimates the value function using scalable statistical and machine learning models:
    • Linear models, deep neural networks, decision trees, and general regression techniques.
  • Error Management Mechanisms:
    • Eligibility Traces: Accelerates credit assignment and temporal consistency across multi-step transitions.
    • Experience Replay: Stores transition tuples in a replay buffer and samples them randomly to break data correlation and stabilize value approximation.

Bellman Equation​

vπ(s)=Eπ[Rt+1⏟Immediate Reward+γvπ(St+1)⏟Discounted Future Value  |  St=s⏟Starting at state s]v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \underbrace{R_{t+1}}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{v_\pi(S_{t+1})}_{\text{Discounted Future Value}} \;\middle|\; \underbrace{S_t = s}_{\text{Starting at state s}} \right]vπ​(s)=Eπ​​Immediate RewardRt+1​​​+γDiscounted Future Valuevπ​(St+1​)​​​Starting at state sSt​=s​​​

  • Fundamental concept in RL using a recursive equation to express a way to compute the value of a state based on the values of its successor states.
v(s)=E[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+…  |  St=s]=E[Rt+1+γ(Rt+2+γRt+3+… )⏟Gt+1  |  St=s]=E[Rt+1+γGt+1  |  St=s]=E[Rt+1+γv(St+1)  |  St=s]=E[Rt+1∣St=s]⏟Immediate Reward R(s)+γ E[v(St+1)∣St=s]⏟Expected Next State Value(∵E[X+γY]=E[X]+γE[Y])=R(s)+γ∑s′P(s′∣s)v(s′)⏟Transition Dynamics(∵E[g(X)]=∑xP(x)g(x))\begin{aligned} v(s) &= \mathbb{E} \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \dots \;\middle|\; S_t = s \right] \\[8pt] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma \underbrace{\left( R_{t+2} + \gamma R_{t+3} + \dots \right)}_{G_{t+1}} \;\middle|\; S_t = s \right] \\[8pt] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1} \;\middle|\; S_t = s \right] \\[8pt] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma v(S_{t+1}) \;\middle|\; S_t = s \right] \\[8pt] &= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} \mid S_t = s]}_{\text{Immediate Reward } \mathcal{R}(s)} + \gamma \, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[v(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s]}_{\text{Expected Next State Value}} && (\because \mathbb{E}[X + \gamma Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \gamma\mathbb{E}[Y]) \\[10pt] &= \mathcal{R}(s) + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}(s' \mid s) v(s')}_{\text{Transition Dynamics}} && \left(\because \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x P(x)g(x)\right) \end{aligned}v(s)​=E[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+…​St​=s]=E​Rt+1​+γGt+1​(Rt+2​+γRt+3​+…)​​​St​=s​=E[Rt+1​+γGt+1​∣St​=s]=E[Rt+1​+γv(St+1​)∣St​=s]=Immediate Reward R(s)E[Rt+1​∣St​=s]​​+γExpected Next State ValueE[v(St+1​)∣St​=s]​​=R(s)+γTransition Dynamicss′∑​P(s′∣s)v(s′)​​​​(∵E[X+γY]=E[X]+γE[Y])(∵E[g(X)]=x∑​P(x)g(x))​

Bellman Equation Example​

v(sBL)=7+γ(0.1⋅v(sBL)+0.5⋅(sTL)+0.4⋅(sBR))v(s_{\text{BL}}) = 7 + \gamma(0.1 \cdot v(s_{\text{BL}}) + 0.5 \cdot(s_{TL}) + 0.4 \cdot(s_{BR})) v(sBL​)=7+γ(0.1⋅v(sBL​)+0.5⋅(sTL​)+0.4⋅(sBR​))

Bellman Equation in Matrix Form​

v=R+γPvv = \mathcal{R} + \gamma \mathcal{P} vv=R+γPv

[v(s1)⋮v(sn)]⏟V of a particular state=[R(s1)⋮R(sn)]⏟Immediate Reward+γ[P11⋯P1n⋮⋱⋮Pn1⋯Pnn]⏟Transition Matrix[v(s1)⋮v(sn)]⏟V of future state\begin{aligned} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} v(s_1) \\ \vdots \\ v(s_n) \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{V of a particular state}} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{R}(s_1) \\ \vdots \\ \mathcal{R}(s_n) \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{P}_{11} & \cdots & \mathcal{P}_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \mathcal{P}_{n1} & \cdots & \mathcal{P}_{nn} \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{Transition Matrix}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} v(s_1) \\ \vdots \\ v(s_n) \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{V of future state}} \end{aligned}V of a particular state​v(s1​)⋮v(sn​)​​​​=Immediate Reward​R(s1​)⋮R(sn​)​​​​+γTransition Matrix​P11​⋮Pn1​​⋯⋱⋯​P1n​⋮Pnn​​​​​V of future state​v(s1​)⋮v(sn​)​​​​​

Solving the Bellman Equation​

Linear System of Equations​

v=R+γPvv−γPv=R(I−γP)v=Rv=(I−γP)−1R\begin{aligned} \mathcal{v} &= \mathcal{R} + \gamma \mathcal{P}\mathcal{v} \\ \mathcal{v} - \gamma \mathcal{P}\mathcal{v} &= \mathcal{R} \\ (I - \gamma \mathcal{P})\mathcal{v} &= \mathcal{R} \\ \mathcal{v} &= (I - \gamma \mathcal{P})^{-1} \mathcal{R} \end{aligned}vv−γPv(I−γP)vv​=R+γPv=R=R=(I−γP)−1R​
  • Computational Complexity: O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3)
  • For small MDPs: direct solution is possible (up to 100 states)
  • For large MDPs:
    • Iterative methods
    • Dynamic Programming
    • Monte Carlo Tree
    • TD learning

State-Value Function​

vπ(s)⏟Value of state s=Eπ⏟Follows policy π[Rt+1⏟Immediate Reward+γvπ(St+1)⏟Discounted Value of Next State  |  St=s⏟Starting at state s]\begin{aligned} \underbrace{v_\pi(s)}_{\text{Value of state } s} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_\pi}_{\text{Follows policy } \pi} \left[ \underbrace{R_{t+1}}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{v_\pi(S_{t+1})}_{\text{Discounted Value of Next State}} \;\middle|\; \underbrace{S_t = s}_{\text{Starting at state } s} \right] \end{aligned}Value of state svπ​(s)​​=Follows policy πEπ​​​​Immediate RewardRt+1​​​+γDiscounted Value of Next Statevπ​(St+1​)​​​Starting at state sSt​=s​​​​
  • Evaluates the expected return starting from state sss and following policy π\piπ thereafter.
  • How good is it to be in state sss?
  • vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s): Expected cumulative return starting from state sss under policy π\piπ.
  • Eπ\mathbb{E}_\piEπ​: Expectation over action selections (At∼πA_t \sim \piAt​∼π) and transition dynamics (St+1∼PS_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{P}St+1​∼P).
  • Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​: Immediate reward received upon transitioning out of state sss.
  • γvπ(St+1)\gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1})γvπ​(St+1​): Discounted expected value of the next successor state St+1S_{t+1}St+1​.
  • St=sS_t = sSt​=s: Condition that the agent starts at state sss at time step ttt.

vπ(s)=∑a∈Aπ(a∣s)qπ(s,a)v_{\pi}(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a \mid s) q_{\pi}(s, a)vπ​(s)=∑a∈A​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a)

  • The value of state sss is the policy-weighted average of the values of all possible actions that can be taken from that state.

Action-Value Function​

qπ(s,a)⏟Action-Value of (s,a)=Eπ⏟Follows policy π[Rt+1⏟Immediate Reward+γqπ(St+1,At+1)⏟Discounted Next Action-Value  |  St=s,At=a⏟Starting at s taking action a]\begin{aligned} \underbrace{q_\pi(s, a)}_{\text{Action-Value of } (s, a)} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_\pi}_{\text{Follows policy } \pi} \left[ \underbrace{R_{t+1}}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{q_\pi(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})}_{\text{Discounted Next Action-Value}} \;\middle|\; \underbrace{S_t = s, A_t = a}_{\text{Starting at } s \text{ taking action } a} \right] \end{aligned}Action-Value of (s,a)qπ​(s,a)​​=Follows policy πEπ​​​​Immediate RewardRt+1​​​+γDiscounted Next Action-Valueqπ​(St+1​,At+1​)​​​Starting at s taking action aSt​=s,At​=a​​​​
  • Evaluates the expected return of taking an arbitrary action aaa in state sss, and subsequently following policy π\piπ from step t+1t+1t+1 onward.
  • How good is it to take action aaa in state sss?

  • Eπ\mathbb{E}_\piEπ​: Expectation over the next transition (St+1∼PS_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{P}St+1​∼P) and the subsequent action (At+1∼πA_{t+1} \sim \piAt+1​∼π).

  • Evaluates state sss directly by averaging over all possible action branches (π\piπ) and their subsequent environmental transitions (P\mathcal{P}P).

Bellman Expectation Equation​

qπ(s,a)=Rsa+γ∑s′∈SPss′a∑a′∈Aπ(a′∣s′)qπ(s′,a′)\begin{aligned} q_\pi(s, a) = \mathcal{R}_s^a + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a \sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a' \mid s') q_\pi(s', a') \end{aligned}qπ​(s,a)=Rsa​+γs′∈S∑​Pss′a​a′∈A∑​π(a′∣s′)qπ​(s′,a′)​
  • Evaluates the state-action pair (s,a)(s, a)(s,a) by summing immediate reward and the expected value of future action pairs (s′,a′)(s', a')(s′,a′), averaged across transition dynamics P\mathcal{P}P and next-step policy choices π\piπ.
  • Rsa\mathcal{R}_s^aRsa​: Immediate reward resulting from the state-action pair (s,a)(s, a)(s,a).
  • γ∑s′∈SPss′a∑a′∈Aπ(a′∣s′)qπ(s′,a′)\gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a \sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a' \mid s') q_\pi(s', a')γ∑s′∈S​Pss′a​∑a′∈A​π(a′∣s′)qπ​(s′,a′): Discounted expected value of the successor state-action pair (s′,a′)(s', a')(s′,a′) resulting from the state-action pair (s,a)(s, a)(s,a).
  • Pss′a\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^aPss′a​: Probability of transitioning from state sss to state s′s's′ when action aaa is taken.
  • S\mathcal{S}S: Set of all possible states.
  • A\mathcal{A}A: Set of all possible actions.
  • π(a′∣s′)\pi(a' \mid s')π(a′∣s′): Probability of taking action a′a'a′ in state s′s's′ under policy π\piπ.
vπ(s)→Action Policy πqπ(s,a)↑↓Environment Transition Pvπ(s′)←Environment Transition Pqπ(s′,a′)\begin{matrix} v_\pi(s) & \xrightarrow{\text{Action Policy } \pi} & q_\pi(s, a) \\ \uparrow & & \downarrow \text{Environment Transition } \mathcal{P} \\ v_\pi(s') & \xleftarrow{\text{Environment Transition } \mathcal{P}} & q_\pi(s', a') \end{matrix}vπ​(s)↑vπ​(s′)​Action Policy π​Environment Transition P​​qπ​(s,a)↓Environment Transition Pqπ​(s′,a′)​

Optimal Value Function​

V∗(s)=max⁡πvπ(s)V_*(s) = \max_\pi v_\pi(s)V∗​(s)=maxπ​vπ​(s)

  • The optimal State-Value Function V∗(s)V_*(s)V∗​(s)
  • Maximum value function over all policies, or maximum possible reward that can be achieved from state sss.

q∗(s,a)=max⁡πqπ(s,a)q_*(s, a) = \max_\pi q_\pi(s, a)q∗​(s,a)=maxπ​qπ​(s,a)

  • The Optimal Action-Value Function q∗(s,a)q_*(s, a)q∗​(s,a)
  • Maximum action-value function over all policies, or given state sss and action taken aaa, what is the maximum reward that can be achieved from there onwards.

Optimal Policy​

π∗≥π  ⟺  vπ∗(s)≥vπ(s)∀s∈S\pi_* \geq \pi \iff v_{\pi_*(s)} \geq v_\pi(s) \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S}π∗​≥π⟺vπ∗​(s)​≥vπ​(s)∀s∈S

  • If certain policy is better than another policy, then the value of the better policy is greater than or equal to the value of others in all states.

Theorem fo any MDP​

  • Existence of an Optimal Policy: There always exists at least one optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​ that is better than or equal to all other policies across all states (π∗≥π,  ∀π\pi_* \ge \pi, \; \forall \piπ∗​≥π,∀π).
  • Uniqueness of the Optimal State-Value Function: Although multiple distinct optimal policies may exist (e.g., when two different paths yield the exact same maximum expected return), all optimal policies achieve the exact same unique optimal state-value function (vπ∗(s)=v∗(s)v_{\pi_*}(s) = v_*(s)vπ∗​​(s)=v∗​(s)).
  • Uniqueness of the Optimal Action-Value Function: Similarly, all optimal policies achieve the exact same unique optimal action-value function (qπ∗(s,a)=q∗(s,a)q_{\pi_*}(s, a) = q_*(s, a)qπ∗​​(s,a)=q∗​(s,a)).

Finding an Optimal Policy​

π∗(a∣s)={1if a=arg⁡max⁡a∈Aq∗(s,a)0otherwise\pi_*(a \mid s) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } a = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} q_*(s, a) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}π∗​(a∣s)={10​if a=argmaxa∈A​q∗​(s,a)otherwise​
  • If q∗(s,a)q_*(s, a)q∗​(s,a) is known, optimal policy is achieved.
  • A deterministic optimal policy always exists for any MDP.

Bellman Optimality Equation​

Bellman Optimality Equation for v∗v_*v∗​​

v∗(s)⏟Optimal Value of State s=max⁡a∈Aq∗(s,a)⏟Optimal Value of Action a\begin{aligned} \underbrace{v_*(s)}_{\text{Optimal Value of State } s} = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \underbrace{q_*(s, a)}_{\text{Optimal Value of Action } a} \end{aligned}Optimal Value of State sv∗​(s)​​=a∈Amax​Optimal Value of Action aq∗​(s,a)​​​
  • State-Value to Action-Value (s→as \rightarrow as→a)
  • The optimal state-value is achieved by greedily picking the single action that yields the maximum optimal action-value.
q∗(s,a)⏟Optimal Action-Value=Rsa⏟Immediate Reward+γ∑s′∈SPss′av∗(s′)⏟Expected Optimal Future Value\begin{aligned} \underbrace{q_*(s, a)}_{\text{Optimal Action-Value}} = \underbrace{\mathcal{R}_s^a}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a v_*(s')}_{\text{Expected Optimal Future Value}} \end{aligned}Optimal Action-Valueq∗​(s,a)​​=Immediate RewardRsa​​​+γExpected Optimal Future Values′∈S∑​Pss′a​v∗​(s′)​​​
  • Action-Value to Next State-Value (a→s′a \rightarrow s'a→s′)
  • Once the action aaa is committed, the outcome is governed by the environment dynamics Pss′a\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^aPss′a​, requiring an expectation (average) over possible successor states s′s's′.
v∗(s)⏟Optimal Value of State s=max⁡a∈A(Rsa⏟Immediate Reward+γ∑s′∈SPss′av∗(s′)⏟Expected Optimal Future Value)\begin{aligned} \underbrace{v_*(s)}_{\text{Optimal Value of State } s} = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \left( \underbrace{\mathcal{R}_s^a}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a v_*(s')}_{\text{Expected Optimal Future Value}} \right) \end{aligned}Optimal Value of State sv∗​(s)​​=a∈Amax​​Immediate RewardRsa​​​+γExpected Optimal Future Values′∈S∑​Pss′a​v∗​(s′)​​​​
  • Bellman Optimality Equation for v∗v_*v∗​ (s→a→s′s \rightarrow a \rightarrow s's→a→s′)
  • Combines the agent's deterministic maximization (max⁡a\max_amaxa​) with the environment's stochastic transition (∑s′Pss′a\sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a∑s′​Pss′a​).
    • It means a structure where the best choice I can make (max⁡\maxmax) embeds the probabilistic outcomes of the world (∑\sum∑) in its calculation.
  • Non-Linear System: Because of the max⁡\maxmax operator, this system of equations cannot be solved directly via matrix inversion (I−γP)−1(I - \gamma\mathcal{P})^{-1}(I−γP)−1
    • it must be solved iteratively via Dynamic Programming (Value Iteration) or Reinforcement Learning.

Bellman Optimality Equation for q∗q_*q∗​​

q∗(s,a)⏟Optimal Action-Value=Rsa⏟Immediate Reward+γ∑s′∈SPss′a⏟Transition Dynamicsmax⁡a′∈Aq∗(s′,a′)⏟Optimal Successor Action\begin{aligned} \underbrace{q_*(s, a)}_{\text{Optimal Action-Value}} = \underbrace{\mathcal{R}_s^a}_{\text{Immediate Reward}} + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a}_{\text{Transition Dynamics}} \underbrace{\max_{a' \in \mathcal{A}} q_*(s', a')}_{\text{Optimal Successor Action}} \end{aligned}Optimal Action-Valueq∗​(s,a)​​=Immediate RewardRsa​​​+γTransition Dynamicss′∈S∑​Pss′a​​​Optimal Successor Actiona′∈Amax​q∗​(s′,a′)​​​
  • Bellman Optimality Equation for q∗q_*q∗​ ((s,a)→s′→a′(s, a) \to s' \to a'(s,a)→s′→a′)
  • Action Commitment: The initial state sss and action aaa are fixed, receiving immediate reward Rsa\mathcal{R}_s^aRsa​.
  • Stochastic Transition: The agent transitions to successor state s′s's′ according to the environment's transition probability Pss′a\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^aPss′a​.
  • Greedy Successor Action (max⁡a′\max_{a'}maxa′​): Upon landing in state s′s's′, the agent greedily selects the action a′a'a′ that yields the maximum possible optimal action-value q∗(s′,a′)q_*(s', a')q∗​(s′,a′).
  • Core Foundation of Q-Learning: This equation directly forms the update target for off-policy algorithms like Q-Learning and DQN

Solving Bellman optimality equation​

  • Non-Linear equation: The optimality equations embed the non-linear max⁡\maxmax operator, they cannot be linearized into standard matrix inversions.

Dynamic Programming Approaches​

πk+1(s)=arg⁡max⁡a∈A[Rsa+γ∑s′∈SPss′avπk(s′)]\begin{aligned} \pi_{k+1}(s) = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \left[ \mathcal{R}_s^a + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a v_{\pi_k}(s') \right] \end{aligned}πk+1​(s)=arga∈Amax​[Rsa​+γs′∈S∑​Pss′a​vπk​​(s′)]​
  • Policy Iteration: Alternates between full Policy Evaluation and Policy Improvement until the policy stabilizes (πk+1=πk\pi_{k+1} = \pi_kπk+1​=πk​).
vk+1(s)←max⁡a∈A[Rsa+γ∑s′∈SPss′avk(s′)]\begin{aligned} v_{k+1}(s) \leftarrow \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \left[ \mathcal{R}_s^a + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a v_k(s') \right] \end{aligned}vk+1​(s)←a∈Amax​[Rsa​+γs′∈S∑​Pss′a​vk​(s′)]​
  • Value Iteration: Turns the Bellman Optimality Equation directly into an iterative update rule, bypassing explicit policy evaluation steps.

Temporal-Difference Control Approaches​

Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γmax⁡aQ(St+1,a)⏟Off-policy Target from q∗−Q(St,At)]\begin{aligned} Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha \left[ \underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a} Q(S_{t+1}, a)}_{\text{Off-policy Target from } q_*} - Q(S_t, A_t) \right] \end{aligned}Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α​Off-policy Target from q∗​Rt+1​+γamax​Q(St+1​,a)​​−Q(St​,At​)​​
  • Q-Learning (Off-Policy TD Control): Learns optimal action-values q∗q_*q∗​ directly from experience tuples (St,At,Rt+1,St+1)(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1})(St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​) by approximating the Bellman Optimality Equation via bootstrapping.
Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γQ(St+1,At+1)⏟On-policy Target from qπ−Q(St,At)]\begin{aligned} Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha \left[ \underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})}_{\text{On-policy Target from } q_\pi} - Q(S_t, A_t) \right] \end{aligned}Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α​On-policy Target from qπ​Rt+1​+γQ(St+1​,At+1​)​​−Q(St​,At​)​​
  • SARSA (On-Policy TD Control): Learns action-values qπq_\piqπ​ for the current policy from experience transitions (St,At,Rt+1,St+1,At+1)(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})(St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​,At+1​), steadily improving the policy toward optimality.

Policy Evaluation​

  • Evaluate a given policy π\piπ is a prediction problem.
  • Iterative application of Bellman Expectation backup.
Input:π:Policy to be evaluatedParameters:θ>0:Small threshold determining estimation accuracyγ∈[0,1]:Discount factorInitialize:V(s)∈R,∀s∈SV(terminal)=0Repeat:Δ←0For each s∈S:v←V(s)V(s)←∑a∈Aπ(a∣s)(Rsa+γ∑s′∈SPss′aV(s′))Δ←max⁡(Δ,  ∣v−V(s)∣)Until Δ<θOutput:V≈vπ\begin{aligned} &\textbf{Input:} \\ &\quad \pi : \text{Policy to be evaluated} \\[6pt] &\textbf{Parameters:} \\ &\quad \theta > 0 : \text{Small threshold determining estimation accuracy} \\ &\quad \gamma \in [0, 1] : \text{Discount factor} \\[6pt] &\textbf{Initialize:} \\ &\quad V(s) \in \mathbb{R}, \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S} \\ &\quad V(\text{terminal}) = 0 \\[8pt] &\textbf{Repeat:} \\ &\quad \Delta \leftarrow 0 \\ &\quad \textbf{For each } s \in \mathcal{S}: \\ &\quad\quad v \leftarrow V(s) \\ &\quad\quad V(s) \leftarrow \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a \mid s) \left( \mathcal{R}_s^a + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a V(s') \right) \\ &\quad\quad \Delta \leftarrow \max \left( \Delta, \; |v - V(s)| \right) \\ &\textbf{Until } \Delta < \theta \\[8pt] &\textbf{Output:} \\ &\quad V \approx v_\pi \end{aligned}​Input:π:Policy to be evaluatedParameters:θ>0:Small threshold determining estimation accuracyγ∈[0,1]:Discount factorInitialize:V(s)∈R,∀s∈SV(terminal)=0Repeat:Δ←0For each s∈S:v←V(s)V(s)←a∈A∑​π(a∣s)(Rsa​+γs′∈S∑​Pss′a​V(s′))Δ←max(Δ,∣v−V(s)∣)Until Δ<θOutput:V≈vπ​​
  • π\piπ: Target policy being evaluated (π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s) is the action selection probability).
  • θ\thetaθ: Small threshold (θ>0\theta > 0θ>0) defining the stopping criterion for convergence.
  • γ\gammaγ: Discount factor (γ∈[0,1]\gamma \in [0, 1]γ∈[0,1]) for future rewards.
  • V(s)V(s)V(s): Current estimated value of state sss (with V(terminal)=0V(\text{terminal}) = 0V(terminal)=0).
  • Δ\DeltaΔ: Maximum absolute value change across all states during the current sweep (max⁡∣v−V(s)∣\max |v - V(s)|max∣v−V(s)∣).
  • Rsa\mathcal{R}_s^aRsa​: Expected immediate reward from taking action aaa in state sss.
  • Pss′a\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^aPss′a​: Transition probability to successor state s′s's′ from state sss via action aaa.
  • vπv_\pivπ​: True state-value function under policy π\piπ that V(s)V(s)V(s) converges to.

Policy Improvement​

π′(s)=arg⁡max⁡a∈A[Rsa+γ∑s′∈SPss′aVπ(s′)]⏟qπ(s,a)\begin{aligned} \pi'(s) = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \underbrace{\left[ \mathcal{R}_s^a + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a V_\pi(s') \right]}_{q_\pi(s, a)} \end{aligned}π′(s)=arga∈Amax​qπ​(s,a)[Rsa​+γs′∈S∑​Pss′a​Vπ​(s′)]​​​
  • Computing Value-function for a policy helps to find better policies.
  • Evaluate the policy π\piπ, find Vπ(s)V_\pi(s)Vπ​(s)
  • Improve the policy by greedy action: π′=greedy(Vπ)\pi' = \text{greedy}(V_\pi)π′=greedy(Vπ​)
  • π\piπ: Current baseline policy before improvement.
  • Vπ(s)V_\pi(s)Vπ​(s): True state-value function evaluated under policy π\piπ.
  • π′\pi'π′: New, improved policy updated via greedy action selection.
  • arg⁡max⁡a\arg\max_{a}argmaxa​: The operation of selecting the action aaa that maximizes the subsequent expected return (qπ(s,a)q_\pi(s, a)qπ​(s,a)).
  • Rsa\mathcal{R}_s^aRsa​: Immediate expected reward earned by taking action aaa in state sss.
  • γ\gammaγ: Discount factor (γ∈[0,1]\gamma \in [0, 1]γ∈[0,1]).
  • Pss′a\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^aPss′a​: Transition probability to successor state s′s's′ from state sss via action aaa.

Policy Iteration Algorithm​

Policy Iteration = Evaluate -> Improve -> Repeat

1. InitializationV(s)∈R and π(s)∈A(s) arbitrarily for all s∈S2. Policy EvaluationLoop:Δ←0Loop for each s∈S:v←V(s)V(s)←∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,π(s))[r+γV(s′)]Δ←max⁡(Δ,  ∣v−V(s)∣)until Δ<θ(θ>0, small positive threshold)3. Policy Improvementpolicy-stable←trueFor each s∈S:old-action←π(s)π(s)←arg⁡max⁡a∈A(s)∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γV(s′)]if old-action≠π(s) then policy-stable←falseif policy-stable then stop and return V≈v∗ and π≈π∗else go to 2\begin{aligned} &\textbf{1. Initialization} \\ &\quad V(s) \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } \pi(s) \in \mathcal{A}(s) \text{ arbitrarily for all } s \in \mathcal{S} \\[6pt] &\textbf{2. Policy Evaluation} \\ &\quad \textbf{Loop:} \\ &\quad\quad \Delta \leftarrow 0 \\ &\quad\quad \textbf{Loop for each } s \in \mathcal{S}: \\ &\quad\quad\quad v \leftarrow V(s) \\ &\quad\quad\quad V(s) \leftarrow \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, \pi(s)) \left[ r + \gamma V(s') \right] \\ &\quad\quad\quad \Delta \leftarrow \max \left( \Delta, \; |v - V(s)| \right) \\ &\quad \textbf{until } \Delta < \theta \quad \text{($\theta > 0$, small positive threshold)} \\[6pt] &\textbf{3. Policy Improvement} \\ &\quad \textit{policy-stable} \leftarrow \text{true} \\ &\quad \textbf{For each } s \in \mathcal{S}: \\ &\quad\quad \textit{old-action} \leftarrow \pi(s) \\ &\quad\quad \pi(s) \leftarrow \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}(s)} \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a) \left[ r + \gamma V(s') \right] \\ &\quad\quad \textbf{if } \textit{old-action} \neq \pi(s) \textbf{ then } \textit{policy-stable} \leftarrow \text{false} \\[4pt] &\quad \textbf{if } \textit{policy-stable} \textbf{ then stop and return } V \approx v_* \text{ and } \pi \approx \pi_* \\ &\quad \textbf{else go to 2} \end{aligned}​1. InitializationV(s)∈R and π(s)∈A(s) arbitrarily for all s∈S2. Policy EvaluationLoop:Δ←0Loop for each s∈S:v←V(s)V(s)←s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,π(s))[r+γV(s′)]Δ←max(Δ,∣v−V(s)∣)until Δ<θ(θ>0, small positive threshold)3. Policy Improvementpolicy-stable←trueFor each s∈S:old-action←π(s)π(s)←arga∈A(s)max​s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γV(s′)]if old-action=π(s) then policy-stable←falseif policy-stable then stop and return V≈v∗​ and π≈π∗​else go to 2​
  • Policy Evaluation (Prediction): What happens if I follow this policy?
  • Vπ(s)V_\pi(s)Vπ​(s): How good is each state?
  • Qπ(s,a)Q_\pi(s,a)Qπ​(s,a): What happens if I take an action aaa?
  • Policy Improvement: Which action is better?
  • Optimal Policy: Repeat until no change

Markov Property​

  • The future is independent of the past given the present state.
  • The current state is sufficient to determine the future, without history.

Markov State​

P[St+1∣St]=P[St+1=s′∣St=s]P[S_{t+1} | S_t] = P[S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s]P[St+1​∣St​]=P[St+1​=s′∣St​=s]

  • ttt: Time step
  • St+1S_{t+1}St+1​: Next state
  • StS_tSt​: Current state
  • S1,…,StS_1, \ldots, S_tS1​,…,St​: History (All previous states)

State Transition Probability​

Pss′=P[St+1=s′∣St=s]P_{ss'} = P[S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s]Pss′​=P[St+1​=s′∣St​=s]

  • Likelihood or probability of moving from one state sss to another state s′s's′ in the next time step t+1t+1t+1.
  • sss: Markov State
  • s′s's′: Successor State
  • ttt: Time step
  • State transition matrix PPP defines the transitions probabilities between all states sss to all successor states s′s's′.

State Transition Matrix​

P=s1…sn←(to state)s1⋮sn[P11…P1n⋮⋱⋮Pn1…Pnn]↑(from state)\mathcal{P} = \begin{array}{rl} & \begin{matrix} \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{s_1}} & \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{\dots}} & \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{s_n}} \end{matrix} \quad \leftarrow \text{(to state)} \\ \begin{matrix} \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{s_1}} \\ \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{\vdots}} \\ \textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{s_n}} \end{matrix} & \hspace{-10pt} \begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{P}_{11} & \dots & \mathcal{P}_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \mathcal{P}_{n1} & \dots & \mathcal{P}_{nn} \end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{matrix} \uparrow \\[-2pt] \mathclap{\text{(from state)}} \end{matrix} & \end{array}P=s1​⋮sn​​↑(from state)​​s1​​…​sn​​←(to state)​P11​⋮Pn1​​…⋱…​P1n​⋮Pnn​​​​
  • State transition matrix PPP defines the transition probabilities between all states sss to all successor states s′s's′.
  • Probability of moving from state sns_nsn​ to s1s_1s1​ is Pn1\mathcal{P}_{n1}Pn1​.

Math cal​

Reinforcement Learning and Math Major Symbols

  • P\mathcal{P}P: Transition Probability Matrix
  • S\mathcal{S}S: State Space
  • A\mathcal{A}A: Action Space
  • R\mathcal{R}R: Reward Function
  • L\mathcal{L}L: Loss Function
  • N(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)N(μ,σ2): Normal Distribution
  • D\mathcal{D}D: Dataset
  • H\mathcal{H}H: Entropy / Hypothesis Space

Markov Process​

Markov Chain

  • What is going to be happened next?
  • it goes through a sequence of states overtime.
  • Stochastic Process: The next state St+1S_{t+1}St+1​ is determined by the current state StS_tSt​ and the transition probability matrix PPP that exhibits the Markov Property.
  • Current state is independent of the past states.
  • Memoryless: History of states leading up to the current state is not necessary to predict the next/future state.
  • MP: ⟨S,P⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P}\rangle⟨S,P⟩, What states comes next?, Observer's Perspective.
  • MRP: ⟨S,P,R,γ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle⟨S,P,R,γ⟩, How good/How much reward is this state in the long run?, Evaluator's Perspective.
  • MDP: ⟨S,A,P,R,γ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle⟨S,A,P,R,γ⟩, What action should I take right now to maximize the long-term reward?, Decision Maker's Perspective.

Pss′=P[St+1=s′∣St=s]\mathcal{P}_{ss'} = P[S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s]Pss′​=P[St+1​=s′∣St​=s]

  • SSS: a finite set of states.
  • P\mathcal{P}P: a state transition matrix, defines the transitions probabilities from all states sss to all successor states s′s's′.
  • NO REWARD, NO ACTIONS.

Transition Diagram​

  • Box: where it ends
  • Arrow: transitions
  • Circle: states
  • Number: probability of transitioning to the state
P=[00.10.50.100.30.40.10.500000.50.50000.5000.20.300.70000.30000001]\mathcal{P} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.1 & 0.5 & 0.1 & 0 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.1 & 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.7 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}P=​00.400.50.70​0.10.10.5000​0.50.50.5000​0.1000.200​0000.30.30​0.300001​​
  • S1: Calibration Site
  • S2: Mineral Site
  • S3: Water Site
  • S4: Drill Site
  • S5: Alien Remain Site
  • S6: Lander Site

Markov Chain Episode​

  • A sequence of states from a starting state to a terminal state.
  • S1,S3,S2,S1,S6S_1, S_3, S_2, S_1, S_6S1​,S3​,S2​,S1​,S6​
  • S1,S3,S3,S2,S1,S4,S4,S1,S6S_1, S_3, S_3, S_2, S_1, S_4, S_4, S_1, S_6S1​,S3​,S3​,S2​,S1​,S4​,S4​,S1​,S6​

Episodic Task vs Continuous Task​

FeatureEpisodic TasksContinuing Tasks
TerminationHas a well-defined terminal state (TTT)Runs indefinitely without termination (T=∞T = \inftyT=∞)
Real-World Examples• Video games (e.g., Super Mario: level clear or death)
• Navigation (reaching destination)
• Board games (e.g., Chess: checkmate/draw)		• Smart thermostat (HVAC temperature control)
• 24/7 industrial robotic process control
• Automated trading & server load management
Execution FlowEnvironment resets to a start state once finishedOperates continuously without automatic resets
  • Episodic Tasks: Tasks with a defined end/terminal state.
  • Continuing Tasks: Tasks without a defined end/terminal state.
  • It may require different MDP formulation and solution methods for each type of task.

Markov Reward Process​

Markov Chain + Reward

⟨S,P,R,γ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle⟨S,P,R,γ⟩

  • SSS: a finite set of states.
  • P\mathcal{P}P: a state transition matrix (Transition Dynamics)
  • R\mathcal{R}R: a reward function to compute expected reward from a state.
    • Rs=E[Rt+1∣St=s]\mathcal{R}_s = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} | S_t = s]Rs​=E[Rt+1​∣St​=s]
    • In the state sss, how much reward can you expect to get in the next time step?
  • γ\gammaγ: a discount factor, to balance the immediate and future rewards.
    • γ∈[0,1]\gamma \in [0, 1]γ∈[0,1]

Return​

Gt=Rt+1+Rt+2+⋯+RTG_t = R_{t+1} + R_{t+2} + \cdots + R_TGt​=Rt+1​+Rt+2​+⋯+RT​

  • GtG_tGt​: Goal Reward
    • The sum of the rewards received from time step ttt.
  • Rt+1,Rt+2,…,RTR_{t+1}, R_{t+2}, \ldots, R_TRt+1​,Rt+2​,…,RT​: the sequence of rewards received after time step ttt
  • TTT: terminal state
  • ttt: time step

Discount​

  • The present value of future rewards.
  • γ=0\gamma = 0γ=0: Myopic evaluation for maximizing immediate reward.
  • γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1: Far-sighted/Long-term evaluation for maximizing future reward.

Discounted Return​

Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯+γT−t−1RT=∑k=0∞γkRt+k+1G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots + \gamma^{T-t-1} R_T = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}Gt​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯+γT−t−1RT​=∑k=0∞​γkRt+k+1​

  • GtG_tGt​: Discounted Return
  • γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1: Undiscounted Markov Reward Process, if all sequences terminate (like games)

Value Function​

v(s)=E[Gt∣St=s]v(s) = \mathbb{E}[G_t | S_t = s]v(s)=E[Gt​∣St​=s]

  • The expected return from state sss.
  • How much total reward can you expect to get starting from this state?
  • A function returning the expected cumulative reward starting from state sss

Markov Decision Process​

Markov Reward Process + Actions(Decisions)

⟨S,A,P,R,γ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle⟨S,A,P,R,γ⟩

  • SSS: a finite set of states.
  • A\mathcal{A}A: a finite set of actions.
  • P\mathcal{P}P: a state transition matrix
    • Pss′a=P[St+1=s′∣St=s,At=a]\mathcal{P}_{ss'}^a = P[S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s, A_t = a]Pss′a​=P[St+1​=s′∣St​=s,At​=a]
  • R\mathcal{R}R: a reward function
    • Rsa=E[Rt+1∣St=s,At=a]\mathcal{R}_s^a = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} | S_t = s, A_t = a]Rsa​=E[Rt+1​∣St​=s,At​=a]
  • γ\gammaγ: a discount factor

Policy​

π(a∣s)=P[At=a∣St=s]\pi(a | s) = P[A_t = a | S_t = s]π(a∣s)=P[At​=a∣St​=s]

  • Policy specifies what actions to take in each state.
    • π(left∣wall)=0.8\pi(\text{left} | \text{wall}) = 0.8π(left∣wall)=0.8
    • π(right∣wall)=0.2\pi(\text{right} | \text{wall}) = 0.2π(right∣wall)=0.2
    • π(straight∣wall)=0.0\pi(\text{straight} | \text{wall}) = 0.0π(straight∣wall)=0.0
    • The agent's playbook for any given state.
  • It fully defines the behavior of the agent.
  • MDP's policy does not depends on history, only on the current state.

Value Function of a Policy​

vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t | S_t = s]vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]

  • The state value function vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) is the expected return starting from state sss and following policy π\piπ.
  • How good it is to be in state sss (under policy π\piπ)?

qπ(s,a)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s,At=a]q_\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t | S_t = s, A_t = a]qπ​(s,a)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s,At​=a]

  • The expected return of taking action aaa in state sss, taking action aaa and then following policy π\piπ.
  • qqq: a quality of action aaa in state sss (under policy π\piπ).
FeatureState-Value Function (vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s))Action-Value Function (qπ(s,a)q_\pi(s, a)qπ​(s,a))
Decision FlowFollows policy π\piπ right from state sssCommits to action aaa first, then follows policy π\piπ
Intuitive Question"How good is it to be in this state?""How good is it to take this specific action in this state?"

Solving MDPs​

Goal: Find optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​ that maximizes the expected return.

  • Using Value Iteration or Policy Iteration.
  • Updating value functions and policies iteratively until convergence.
  • Evaluation: Compute the value function vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) for a given policy π\piπ.
  • Improvement: Update the policy π\piπ to choose better actions based on the updated value function.
    • To converge to the optimal value function and policy v∗,π∗v^*, \pi^*v∗,π∗

POMDPs​

MDPs with hidden states.

⟨S,A,O⏟공간 (Spaces),P,R,Z⏟함수 / 규칙 (Functions),γ⏟상수 (Discount Factor)⟩\langle \underbrace{\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{O}}_{\text{공간 (Spaces)}}, \underbrace{\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{Z}}_{\text{함수 / 규칙 (Functions)}}, \underbrace{\gamma}_{\text{상수 (Discount Factor)}} \rangle⟨공간 (Spaces)S,A,O​​,함수 / 규칙 (Functions)P,R,Z​​,상수 (Discount Factor)γ​​⟩

  • SSS: a finite set of states
  • A\mathcal{A}A: a finite set of actions
  • O\mathcal{O}O: a finite set of observations
    • e.g. driving in foggy weather.
  • P\mathcal{P}P: a state transition matrix
  • R\mathcal{R}R: a reward function
  • Z\mathcal{Z}Z: an observation function
    • Zs′,oa=P[Ot+1=o∣St+1=s′,At=a]\mathcal{Z}_{s', o}^a = P[O_{t+1} = o | S_{t+1} = s', A_t = a]Zs′,oa​=P[Ot+1​=o∣St+1​=s′,At​=a]
    • an observation function specifying the probability of receiving observation ooo given state s′s's′ and action aaa
    • After taking action aaa and landing in state s′s's′, how likely is the agent to observe ooo?
  • γ\gammaγ: a discount factor
  • e.g.
    • Robot navigation with noisy/uncalibrated sensors.
    • Autonomous Driving with Sensor uncertainty due to bad weather conditions and unexpected events.

Finite Horizon MDPs​

  • Finite Time Steps (TTT): A sequential decision-making process restricted to a fixed, finite number of steps (TTT) to maximize cumulative rewards.
  • Target Applications: Well-suited for problems with explicit deadlines or time-varying environment dynamics.
  • Decision Basis: Optimal decisions are made using current state (StS_tSt​), available actions (AtA_tAt​), transition probabilities (P\mathcal{P}P), and immediate rewards (R\mathcal{R}R).
  • Representative Example: A robot navigating a grid world with a limited step count or battery budget to reach a goal while avoiding obstacles.
  • Discount Factor (γ\gammaγ): Because the horizon TTT is finite, the cumulative return cannot diverge to infinity, allowing the use of undiscounted formulations (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1).
  • Time-Dependent (Non-Stationary) Policy:
    • Unlike infinite-horizon MDPs, the optimal action depends explicitly on the remaining time steps (T−tT - tT−t).
    • Policy Notation: πt(s)\pi_t(s)πt​(s) (indexed by time step ttt).
    • Intuition: An agent may play conservatively early on, but take high-risk, high-reward actions right before the deadline.
DimensionFinite-Horizon MDPInfinite-Horizon MDP
Time Horizon (TTT)T<∞T < \inftyT<∞ (Explicit terminal step)T→∞T \to \inftyT→∞ (Perpetual / ongoing)
Policy NatureNon-Stationary (πt(s)\pi_t(s)πt​(s), changes over time)Stationary (π(s)\pi(s)π(s), time-invariant)
Discount Factor (γ\gammaγ)γ≤1\gamma \le 1γ≤1 (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 is valid)Typically γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1 required for convergence
Objective Functionmax⁡E[∑t=0TγtRt+1]\max \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{T} \gamma^t R_{t+1} \right]maxE[∑t=0T​γtRt+1​]max⁡E[∑t=0∞γtRt+1]\max \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t R_{t+1} \right]maxE[∑t=0∞​γtRt+1​]

Limitations of MDPs​

  • Markovian Assumption: Assumes future transitions depend solely on the current state StS_tSt​, ignoring past historical trajectories and temporal dependencies that matter in real-world dynamics (e.g., momentum, acceleration).
    • State augmentation, frame stacking, RNN/Transformer, POMDP
  • Complete Knowledge Requirement: Assumes exact a priori knowledge of transition probabilities P\mathcal{P}P and reward functions R\mathcal{R}R, which are rarely accessible without sample-based learning in complex environments.
    • Model-free RL: Q-learning, SARSA, Policy Gradient
  • Finite State and Action Spaces: Restricted to discrete and countable sets, whereas real-world robotics and physical control tasks typically involve continuous states and actions.
    • Function approximation, Actor-Critic: DDPG, TD3, SAC, PPO
  • Curse of Dimensionality: Tabular value and policy storage scale exponentially as state dimensions grow (∣S∣×∣A∣|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{A}|∣S∣×∣A∣), making high-dimensional environments (e.g., raw pixel inputs) computationally intractable.
    • Deep RL: neural approximation of VVV, QQQ, or π\piπ
  • Partial Observability: Assumes full access to the true ground-truth state (Ot=StO_t = S_tOt​=St​), failing to account for real-world sensor noise, occlusions, and incomplete observations.
    • POMDP, belief-state estimation, recurrent policies
